items.title: Lahore High Court rules against divorce-linked Quran oath
items.description: LAHORE: The Lahore High Court has held that an offer to settle a civil dispute through a “special oath” on the Holy Quran, coupled with a condition of divorce if the oath is false, is not a lawful offer. Justice Anwaar Hussain issued the ruling allowing a civil revision filed by Muhammad Azam Khan against Akhtar Khan and others. During a pending appeal before an appellate court, the petitioner had offered in August 2023 to have the matter decided by an oath on the Holy Quran taken by the opposing side, with a condition that the oath-taker’s wife would stand divorced if the oath proved false. On Aug 22, the respondents appeared before the appellate court and expressed willingness to take the oath, while the petitioner said he did not wish to proceed. Says divorce clause renders special oath offer unlawful; sets aside order refusing withdrawal of special oath offer He formally applied to withdraw the offer on Aug 24, when the respondents accepted the oath but rejected the divorce condition. The appellate court dismissed his withdrawal application in September 2023, ruling that the offer had been accepted. It also directed that the oath be taken on the Holy Quran alone, holding the divorce stipulation contrary to public policy. Justice Hussain held that the appellate court erred. He maintained a special oath is not a mere private contract but a procedure governed by the Oaths Act, 1873. Section 8 of the Act permits only oaths that are not repugnant to justice or decency and do not affect any third person. A condition tying a perjury penalty to the oath-taker’s wife’s divorce violated both limits, the judge said. The judge noted that, even if the offer was valid, the respondents’ reply was not absolute. Assisting the court as amicus curiae, Barrister Awais Arshad, submitted that an offer for special oath must be examined not only under the 1873 Act, but also in the light of the principles governing offer, acceptance and revocation under the Contract Act, 1872. He said acceptance does not automatically follow an offer and, in the present case, where the petitioner expressed his intention to withdraw the offer during the same proceedings in which the respondents conveyed their acceptance, it cannot be presumed that a concluded agreement had come into existence. Justice Hussain ruled that a court cannot strike out an objectionable condition and enforce the rest against a party who never assented to the altered arrangement. The judge also found that the order sheet of the relevant hearing did not establish whether the petitioner’s refusal came before or after the respondents’ willingness. He further noted that a claim that one respondent had travelled from abroad specifically for the oath collapsed when his passport was summoned and the counsel acknowledged he was already in Pakistan. The judge allowed the petition and set aside the appellate court’s order that had refused to let the petitioner withdraw the offer. The judge directed the appellate court to decide the appeal on its merits without treating the proposed oath as binding on the petitioner. Published in Dawn, October 28th, 2026

items.title: FG kicks off $100m Southeast gas pipeline project
items.description: …As SEDC seals deal with GasSync, commits $3m .. Tinubu says S’East must rise from potential to reality …Mbah, governors hail Tinubu, pledge support for 400km pipeline The Federal Government, through the South East Development Commission (SEDC) has kicked off a $100 million gas distribution pipeline project to boost industrialisation, attract investments and create jobs in the South East. The 400-kilometre pipeline, designed to connect gas resources to industrial and commercial centres across Enugu, Anambra, Imo, Abia and Ebonyi states, has about 150 potential customers identified, with projected demand of 254 million standard cubic feet of gas per day. The investment agreement for the project was signed on Tuesday at the South-East Gas Infrastructure Investment and Project Development Ceremony held at Hotel Presidential, Enugu, marking a significant step towards establishing a regional gas distribution network. Tinubu, represented by the Deputy Speaker of the House of Representatives, Benjamin Kalu, described the project as a strategic investment that would connect the region’s natural gas resources to industries, strengthen manufacturing and unlock economic opportunities across the five states. “The Southeast’s entrepreneurial spirit is one of Nigeria’s greatest economic assets. I have always believed that the prosperity of the Southeast is inseparable from the prosperity of Nigeria,” the President said. He said the project aligned with his administration’s commitment to building an integrated regional economy, stressing that gas infrastructure should support industrial development across state boundaries rather than serve isolated markets. “Gas infrastructure must therefore serve industries and markets, not stop at political boundaries. That is the economic logic of regional integration,” he said. The President said the pipeline would benefit manufacturers in Aba, strengthen industrial clusters in Nnewi and Onitsha, attract productive enterprises to Enugu, expand agro-processing and manufacturing in Ebonyi and connect Imo’s gas resources to the wider regional economy. He, however, said the ambition extended beyond supplying existing factories to creating the conditions for new industries, industrial parks and investments that had stalled because of unreliable energy supply. “Our ambition is not simply to deliver gas to existing factories. It is to make possible factories that do not yet exist, industrial parks yet to be developed, and investments that have remained on the drawing board because reliable energy was unavailable,” Tinubu said. He described the South-East Development Commission (SEDC) as an institution established to deliver measurable development outcomes, urging it to assess its performance by the investments it mobilised, infrastructure it enabled, opportunities it created and lives it improved. The President said the South-East Vision 2050 development framework, supported by Vice-President Kashim Shettima and the governors of the region, provided a foundation for coordinated economic growth. He also cited his approval of the South-East Investment Company as part of efforts to attract private capital into strategic development projects, noting that governments could not finance every development ambition from public funds. “This is the model I expect from our development institutions: identify strategic economic opportunities, prepare credible projects, commit public resources responsibly and mobilise private capital at a scale government budgets alone cannot achieve,” he said. Tinubu commended the SEDC for committing $3 million to the gas project and establishing a framework to mobilise additional investments from state governments, institutions and private investors. He said the project’s initial phase required approximately $100 million, describing the partnership between public institutions and private investors as essential to developing sustainable infrastructure. “We are not investing in pipelines for their own sake. We are investing in the industries, businesses and jobs those pipelines will make possible,” the President said. He urged the commission and its partners to uphold commercial discipline, transparency, environmental responsibility, community engagement and the highest safety standards throughout the project’s implementation. “The true measure of government’s commitment is not what we promise, but what we deliver,” he said, expressing optimism that the investment would help create an industrial economy capable of competing in African and global markets. Tinubu said the ultimate objective was to translate the region’s natural resources into productive economic activity, employment and improved living standards. “Let the gas beneath our soil power our industries. Let that energy become production. Let production become employment. Let employment become prosperity for our people,” he said. The President urged the SEDC, state governments and project partners to establish clear implementation timelines, measurable milestones and regular progress reports, stressing that the project’s success would ultimately be measured by its ability to attract investments, revive industries, create jobs and improve the economic fortunes of people across the five Southeast states. Enugu State Governor, Dr. Peter Mbah, commended Tinubu for establishing the SEDC, describing the commission as the institutional vehicle needed to realise the Southeast’s longstanding industrialisation aspirations. “Tinubu loves the Igbo. The SEDC is a commission whose time has come. It was an idea conceived many decades ago, but it took President Tinubu to establish this long-awaited dream of industrialisation of the Southeast,” Mbah said. He described the signing of the investment agreement as the commencement of the investment process, adding that the initiative would help realise the region’s aspiration for a common market and coordinated industrial development. “What we have just signed here today is an investment agreement, meaning that investment has commenced,” he said. Mbah, who said he was excited that the project was advancing less than 13 months after he publicly advocated the idea, praised the commission for adopting an innovative financing model that brings governments and private investors together. He said the project would create opportunities for young people to build their futures in the Southeast rather than migrate to other parts of the country in search of jobs. “Before now, it was our young people running out of the region in search of greener pastures. But with what we have now, our young people can sit back and find their future here in the region. This is all thanks to President Tinubu,” he said. The governor assured the SEDC and its partners that the Southeast governors were committed to the pipeline project, promising to expedite right-of-way arrangements and environmental impact assessment approvals. “We, the Southeast governors, are committed to this. We will ensure that the right of way and EIA are given accelerated approval,” he said. Imo State Deputy Governor Lady Chinyere Ekomaru, who represented Governor Hope Uzodimma, commended Tinubu and the SEDC for initiating the project, noting that Imo’s substantial natural gas resources placed the state in a strategic position to benefit. She said the project was coming at an opportune time, particularly as companies were seeking to become offtakers of gas from the Assa North–Ohaji South development. Ekomaru urged residents to consider the Federal Government’s infrastructure investments in the Southeast in making their political choices ahead of the 2027 general elections. “A vote for APC is a direct vote for the continuation of this project. A bird in hand is worth more than 10 in the bush. Let’s reason wisely,” she said. Anambra State Deputy Governor Dr Onyekachukwu Ibezim, representing Governor Chukwuma Soludo, commended the commission but stressed that its success would ultimately be determined by its impact on the people. “We will clap for you when we begin to feel the impact of what you are doing,” he said. Ibezim noted that states across the region had gas resources that could support industrial growth if properly developed. He urged communities along the pipeline route to embrace the project and cooperate with its promoters. “I want to urge the communities through which the pipelines will pass to have a buy-in. We are strongly behind the commission,” he said, while commending the enthusiasm shown by industrialists at the event. Ebonyi State Deputy Governor Mrs Patricia Obila, representing Governor Francis Nwifuru, described energy as fundamental to industrial growth, lamenting that inadequate power supply had contributed to the decline of several enterprises in the region. “Energy is power. Its importance cannot be overemphasised. With it, factories will produce, the economy will blossom and employment will be great,” she said. Obila expressed the Ebonyi government’s readiness to support the project, promising to provide the necessary cooperation to facilitate its implementation and help moribund companies resume operations. “We will give you all the support needed to operate in Ebonyi to ensure that our moribund companies return back to operations,” she said. Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Regional Development, Dr Mary Ogbe, said the SEDC was developing initiatives capable of improving living standards across the Southeast. She assured the governors that the commission would complement their development efforts rather than compete with them, while urging investors to take advantage of the opportunities emerging from the project. Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of SEDC, Mark Okoye, said the commission had conducted technical, financial and legal due diligence before committing funds to the project, which received approval from its governing board. Okoye said the commission was targeting aggregate regional investment participation of up to $30 million, including its initial $3 million commitment, as part of efforts to mobilise the private capital required to advance the project. He said the initiative aligned with the commission’s industrialisation programme and its commitment to developing infrastructure that would benefit the entire region. Representing GasSync, the project promoter, Callistus Mba said the pipeline would connect gas resources close to the Southeast to industrial users across the five states, reducing dependence on the expensive transportation of compressed natural gas (CNG) and liquefied natural gas (LNG) by road. Mba said the proposed network would originate from the Ohaji area of Imo State, run through Owerri and branch towards Aba in Abia State and Onitsha in Anambra State, with extensions to Enugu and Ebonyi. He said the company planned to begin construction at two points simultaneously to accelerate delivery, following concerns raised by Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah that constructing the entire network sequentially from Imo could delay gas supply to other states. “We are going to start at Ohaji and Onitsha at the same time,” Mba said, explaining that the approach would allow construction towards Enugu and Ebonyi to progress alongside work on the Imo and Anambra sections. He said the company had identified about 150 prospective customers across the region and was engaging industries to secure demand for the gas, including manufacturing companies, power-generation facilities and agro-processing businesses. Mba cited Geometric Power in Abia State among the companies with which engagement was already underway. He added that the pipeline would support efforts to revive moribund industries in Enugu and develop agro-processing facilities in Ebonyi. On the project timeline, he said procurement activities had commenced, funding arrangements were advancing towards financial close, and preparations for engineering, procurement and construction were progressing. “We intend to start construction in the first quarter of 2027,” Mba said, projecting that the project would be ready for first gas delivery in the second quarter of 2028, subject to the completion of the necessary requirements. He identified regulatory approvals, right-of-way arrangements, community engagement and coordination among federal and state authorities as critical to meeting the schedule, urging the governors and relevant institutions to facilitate permits and work with host communities along the pipeline route. items.title: L’impact de l’IA sur l’emploi se diffuse au-delà du secteur technologique
items.description: Dans une note envoyée à leurs clients lundi 26 octobre, les économistes de la banque américaine Goldman Sachs estiment qu’il ya des « signes plus nets » qui indiquent que l’impact de l’intelligence artificielle sur l’emploi commence à se propager aux États-Unis en dehors du secteur technologique. Comme le montrent les données du Bureau du recensement et du Bureau des statistiques du travail (BLS), c’est notamment le cas dans les secteurs de l’assurance, de l’immobilier ou de l’intermédiation de crédit, où l’emploi progresse nettement moins vite qu’avant la pandémie de Covid-19. Selon la banque, dans l’ensemble des secteurs non manufacturiers américains, plus la part d’entreprises utilisant l’IA est élevée, plus la croissance de l’emploi est faible et le taux de chômage élevé AI’s labor-market impact is spreading beyond tech, Goldman Sachs says », Seeking Alpha , 27 octobre 2026.'> 1 . La banque estime que la corrélation est statistiquement significative. Si les données publiques confirment le lien avec la croissance de l’emploi, celui avec le chômage apparaît plus fragile. Les sondages montrent désormais que le public américain est particulièrement inquiet quant à l’impact de l’IA sur l’économie et l’emploi. Selon une enquête du Pew Research Center réalisée entre fin septembre et début octobre, la moitié des Américains (50 %) se disent « très préoccupés » par le rôle de l’IA dans l’économie. L’inquiétude sur l’emploi progresse également : 48 % se disent « très préoccupés » par le fait que des personnes souhaitant travailler ne parviennent pas à trouver d’emploi, contre 29 % en octobre 2022 Cost Concerns Dominate as Public’s Economic Ratings Turn More Negative , Pew Research Center, 8 octobre 2026.'> 2 . La recherche d’optimisation des tâches humaines par des outils d’IA n’est pas circonscrite aux entreprises : le gouvernement néerlandais a annoncé lundi 26 octobre la suppression d’environ 25 000 postes dans la fonction publique d’État – soit près de 15 % de ses effectifs. Ces suppressions s’inscrivent dans le cadre d’un plan visant à rendre l’administration « plus simple, plus intelligente et plus petite » Kabinet werkt aan slagvaardige overheid : eenvoudiger, slimmer en kleiner , Gouvernement des Pays-Bas, 26 octobre 2026.'> 3 . Il s’agit du projet le plus ambitieux en matière de déploiement de l’IA mis en place par un gouvernement à ce jour. La Haye table sur 900 millions d’euros d’économies en 2027, et jusqu’à 3,5 milliards par an à partir de 2035. La police et la défense sont pour le moment exemptées. L’article L’impact de l’IA sur l’emploi se diffuse au-delà du secteur technologique est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: US costs of Iran war rise to over $47bn, according to Pentagon estimate
items.description: The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran , more than 25 per cent higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters . The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly. The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years. The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict. More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “ platform losses ,” which include the loss of aircraft, including many drones lost during the war. Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time. Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful. But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible. Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so. The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war. While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.

items.title: PANDEF@10: Leaders push for 50% derivation
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA—THE Pan Niger Delta Forum, PANDEF, the apex socio-political body of the South-South geopolitical zone has called for a total overhaul of the region, demand an increase in the derivation allocation to oil-producing states from the current minimum of 13 percent to 50 percent. It also wants accelerated completion of the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway and urgent environmental remediation across the Niger Delta. PANDEF urged the Federal Government, the Revenue Mobilisation, Allocation and Fiscal Commission, RMAFC, and the National Assembly to initiate measures to raise the allocation to at least 50 percent, just as it argued that the minimum 13 percent derivation allocation had remained unchanged for more than two decades, despite the environmental damage and economic difficulties facing oil-producing communities. Addressing newsmen in Abuja, yesterday, after a meeting of the organisation’s Board of Trustees and National Executive Committee, virtually to mark the 10 years of existence of the organisation, PANDEF National Chairman, Amb. Godknows Igali, said: “The minimum 13 percent derivation allocation had remained unchanged for more than two decades, despite the environmental damage and economic difficulties facing oil-producing communities. We are demanding an upward review to 50 percent. “We also demand the abolition of the onshore/offshore dichotomy in revenue allocation. We insist that offshore oil and gas operations could damage marine ecosystems and fishing grounds relied upon by coastal communities.” The meeting was attended by the Board of Trustees Chairman and former Akwa Ibom State Governor, Obong Victor Attah, former Attorney-General and Minister of Justice, Kanu Agabi, SAN, PANDEF National Publicity Secretary, Minimising Obiuwevbi, alongside political leaders, traditional rulers and other stakeholders from the six South-South states. Further Igali said: “We propose exploring a market-based South-South investment fund to mobilise resources from individuals, businesses, institutions and other stakeholders for investment in critical sectors. The proposed fund would support enterprise development, improve regional connectivity and create jobs, with the organisation planning to engage private-sector players and other partners to develop a workable framework.” On the 2027 elections, he said: “We called on the people of the South-South to exercise their civic responsibilities peacefully and vote according to their conscience, choosing candidates at all levels whose programmes, commitments, and demonstrate capacity align with the aspirations of the region and who can contribute meaningfully to the peace, progress, and development of the Niger Delta. “Also as the country prepares for the elections, we are calling for a framework that extend to environmental remediation to other polluted communities. We urged presidential candidates in the 2027 elections to present measurable and time-bound plans for restoring the region. “The development agenda of the candidates must also address the region’s infrastructure deficit. Also, the completion of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway as non-negotiable.” On the environmental damage in the region, he expressed concern that communities across the Niger Delta continued to bear the consequences of more than six decades of oil and gas exploration, identified Nembe Creek in Bayelsa State, Odidi in Delta State and Kula in Rivers State as areas requiring urgent intervention, while demanding sustained and transparent funding for the Ogoni clean-up programme. “We called for adequate, sustained and transparent funding of the Ogoni clean-up programme. The Federal Government must to develop a comprehensive framework for extending environmental remediation to other affected communities across the region. “While we welcome the Federal Government’s decision to retain the original broad alignment of the 750-kilometre project, the highway could improve connectivity among coastal states, stimulate trade and unlock opportunities in the blue and marine economy.” Further, he said: “We advocate support for modular refineries through appropriate financing, licensing and technical assistance, alongside environmental compliance measures. Modular refineries could complement large-scale refining projects, support local businesses and reduce dependence on imported petroleum products.” The post PANDEF@10: Leaders push for 50% derivation appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Stop using money to manipulate elections — Inusah Fuseini warns vote-buying politicians
items.description: Former Tamale Central Member of Parliament Inusah Fuseini has cautioned against the growing use of money to influence internal party elections, saying financial inducements threaten electoral integrity even when they fail to determine the eventual winner. He said the presence of vote-buying in the recent National Democratic Congress (NDC) constituency executive elections was troubling in itself, warning that political parties risk undermining democratic values when candidates use cash to court delegates. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, October 27, the former member of Parliament’s Constitutional and Legal Affairs Committee said the outcome of the elections showed that spending more money did not necessarily translate into electoral victory. “When we produced our report, we said that we did not believe that the influence of the use of money would influence voters to cast their vote one way or the other. But the fact that it was present was bad in itself,” he said. Mr Fuseini said voters could still exercise independent judgement despite attempts to influence their choices, adding that the experience should serve as a warning to politicians who believe money can secure electoral success. He welcomed comments by a person who had spoken against the practice, saying such a position could discourage candidates from relying on financial inducements to win votes. He said the central concern was not simply whether a candidate who spent heavily won or lost, but whether the use of money had the potential to distort the electoral process. “What we are concerned with is the undue influence that has the potential to corrupt the outcome of elections that affects the integrity of elections,” he said. Mr Fuseini warned that the increasing reliance on money in internal party contests risked shifting attention away from the candidates’ competence, ideas and commitment to public service. He said such a trend could also exclude candidates who lacked the financial resources to compete, regardless of their leadership qualities or support among party members. Voters’ conscience To illustrate his point, Mr Fuseini referred to the election results, arguing that some candidates who reportedly distributed more money than others did not win. He mentioned Babar and Jamal while discussing the results, saying the outcome challenged the assumption that the candidate who spent the most would necessarily emerge victorious. He also cited the case of a candidate who received only one vote and, according to his account, had not given money to voters. “And again I go back to also there was one person who got only one vote, and that person never gave anything,” he said. Mr Fuseini questioned whether the candidate’s failure to distribute money explained the result, while suggesting that voters retained the ability to make their own choices. “Is it because that person never gave anything that he got one vote, and who was this person who voted? That person was a voter of conscience who received but decided that he would act one way or the other and not be influenced by what he had received?” he said. His comments highlight the distinction between the presence of financial inducements and their actual influence on voting decisions. Even where voters reject attempts to influence them, he suggested, the practice remains damaging to the credibility of elections. Safeguarding internal democracy The debate over vote-buying raises broader questions about the conduct of internal party elections and the ability of candidates without substantial financial resources to compete fairly. Although Mr Fuseini said money might not always determine the outcome, he warned that its presence could compromise the integrity of the process and weaken confidence in party democracy. His remarks come at a time when political parties face recurring concerns about the role of cash and other inducements in contests for internal leadership positions. Ensuring transparent elections, enforcing party rules and encouraging delegates to assess candidates on their leadership records and ideas are among the measures that can help strengthen internal democracy.

items.title: Northern Ashanti Mines challenges Minerals Commission over Konongo takeover, disputes $8.3m debt
items.description: Northern Ashanti Mines Limited (NAML) has challenged the Minerals Commission’s justification for taking over its Konongo premises, accusing the regulator of making false claims about its debt and mining activities. In a statement responding to the Commission’s defence of the takeover, the company described the regulator’s account as containing “falsehoods, untruths and half-truths”. NAML said it had invested more than US$100 million in developing the mine since taking it over in 2019. It accused the Commission of acting in bad faith and seeking to undermine a Ghanaian-owned business. The company disputed the Commission’s assertion that it had met the requirements of Section 68 of the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703). According to NAML, it received no notice identifying a statutory breach before the revocation of its mining lease and prospecting licence. It said the only correspondence received was a letter dated April 30, 2026, communicating the revocation. Although that letter referred to an earlier notice, the company maintained that it had not received such a notice. “The Company finds the claim and actions of the Minerals Commission perplexing and in complete bad faith,” the statement said. NAML also challenged the Commission’s claim that the revocation related to debts of US$8,332,000 and US$49,000 associated with its mining lease and prospecting licence, respectively. The company said an audit communication from the Commission in May 2026 put its debt at approximately US$2.4 million. It argued that this was separate from a legacy debt of about US$8.3 million attributed to the mine’s previous operator. NAML said it had paid more than US$1 million towards reducing its outstanding balance. The company said it had requested time to settle its obligations because it was still developing the mine, including constructing a processing plant, and had not begun producing gold or earning revenue. “The Minerals Commission has at no point expressed any disagreement to this proposal,” it said. NAML rejected the claim that it had undertaken no meaningful mining operations on the concession for more than two years. It argued that mine development and investment in processing infrastructure are essential to responsible mining. The company said the Commission had issued permits for projects, including a new processing plant and mining activities to stockpile ore ahead of full production. It cited two permits issued on February 7 and February 17, 2026, both due to expire on December 31, 2026. NAML maintained that it was carrying out mining activities under those permits. The company said it had turned to the courts to protect its investment and its ambition to build an indigenous mining business. It also alleged an emerging pattern of “horrible, unlawful takeovers” of Ghanaian-owned mining assets, which it accused the Commission of instigating or facilitating. Despite the dispute, NAML said it remained open to dialogue and a resolution that would protect confidence in Ghana’s mining investment environment.

items.title: Why 5G remains out of reach for most Nigerians
items.description: •High cost of devices, coverage remains uneven •As smartphone market contracts 11% amid rising device prices •Africa’s budget smartphone shipments plunge 34% amid rising costs By Juliet Umeh Nigeria’s mobile market has shifted significantly towards newer network technologies over the past three years, but 5G remains out of reach for most consumers. High smartphone prices, uneven network coverage and rising infrastructure costs continue to limit adoption, despite growing demand for mobile data. In May 2023, 2G accounted for 58.36 percent of reported mobile connections, while 4G represented 25.06 percent and 5G just 0.12 percent. By August 2026, 4G had become the leading technology at 54.77 percent, while 2G fell to 36.05 percent. 5G increased to 4.92 percent. The data from the Nigerian Communications Commission, NCC, show progress but underline how slowly the newest technology is reaching the wider population. Chief Technology Officer of NATCOM Development and Investment Limited, trading as NTEL, Kingsley Uwazie, said Nigerians had a strong appetite for data consumption, but the cost of accessing 5G remained a significant barrier. “The 5G ecosystem is in its maturity phase. It has been proven that there is an appetite. Nigerians have an appetite to consume data. But there is a barrier to acquiring the devices and using the technology,” he said. High cost of compatible devices Consumers need 5G-enabled smartphones to access the technology, but rising device prices are making upgrades increasingly difficult, particularly for low-income earners. Uwazie said 5G devices remained expensive despite subsidies offered by some operators. “5G, at the moment, is not a cheap technology to deploy or to own. The cost of 5G devices has been high,” he said. He cited MTN Nigeria and Airtel Nigeria as operators subsidising selected devices, adding that a phone available for about N50, 000 with a subsidy could cost more than N200, 000 without it. The affordability challenge has intensified as Nigeria’s smartphone market contracted by 11 percent in the second quarter of 2026, according to technology research firm Omdia. Rising memory-chip costs, partly linked to growing demand from artificial intelligence, AI, data centres, have increased pressure on manufacturers and consumers. Across Africa, shipments of smartphones priced below $100 fell by 34 percent year-on-year during the quarter. In Nigeria, a market assessment published by technology news platform Condia found that prices of selected Tecno, Infinix, Oppo and itel models increased between January and June 2026. The midpoint price of the itel S-Series Ultra rose from about N263, 500 to N316,400, while the Infinix Zero Series increased from approximately N550,000 to N637,500. Omdia warned in June that Nigerian smartphone prices could rise by another 15 to 30 percent through the remainder of 2026 if component costs continued increasing. These developments could discourage consumers from upgrading, slowing the growth of the 5G user base. Coverage remains uneven Even consumers who can afford compatible devices may struggle to access reliable 5G connections because coverage varies by location. MTN’s 2023 pilot announcement identified Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Ibadan, Kano, Owerri and Maiduguri as intended launch cities, subject to coverage. Airtel began its rollout in Lagos, Ogun, Rivers and the Federal Capital Territory, focusing on selected locations. However, a rollout in a city or state does not guarantee availability in every neighbourhood. A December 2025 report based on Ookla analysis put Lagos’s average 5G coverage gap at 55.4 percent, meaning a compatible phone could not connect to 5G for more than half of the measured time. The gap was approximately 50 percent for MTN and 77 percent for Airtel. In Abuja, the average gap stood at 47.4 percent. These figures measure time-based access gaps, not the proportion of land without coverage, but they illustrate the difficulty consumers face in obtaining consistent service. High operating costs slow expansion Expanding 5G requires substantial investment in network infrastructure, electricity and transmission. Operators must determine whether the number of potential subscribers in an area can justify those costs. Uwazie estimated that operating a telecommunications site in Nigeria could cost between $2,000 and $3,000 monthly, compared with about $300 in China and $500 in India. He said the costs included power and transmission. “If you deploy 5G in areas where only two people have 5G-enabled phones, it means those two people can’t cater for the operating expenditure required to deploy 5G. The operating expenditure of running mobile networks in Nigeria is extremely high. It is a combination of both power and transmission, keeping that site up.” The limited number of compatible devices can, therefore, weaken the business case for expanding coverage, particularly in areas where operators expect low subscriber numbers. Digital inclusion at risk The challenge extends beyond 5G adoption to Nigeria’s broader digital inclusion ambitions. The GSMA’s smartphone adoption report found that only 27 percent of Nigeria’s population owned a smartphone in 2024, while the mobile internet usage gap remained close to 60 percent. The NCC said in April 2026 that it was exploring ways to make cheaper smartphones available. Nigeria was also selected for pilot initiatives coordinated by the GSMA’s Handset Affordability Coalition to expand access to affordable 4G smartphones. However, rising global component costs threaten to undermine these efforts. Affordable devices and reliable connectivity are essential for mobile banking, digital education, online commerce and employment opportunities. Expanding network coverage alone will not connect consumers who cannot afford internet-enabled phones. For 5G to reach more Nigerians, compatible devices must become cheaper, coverage must improve and operators must find sustainable ways to reduce deployment costs. Until these barriers are addressed, 5G will remain largely inaccessible to many consumers, with adoption concentrated among those who can afford compatible smartphones and live in well-served locations. Vanguard News The post Why 5G remains out of reach for most Nigerians appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: L’Algérie déploie son armée au Niger : les dessous d’un tournant stratégique
items.description: Les relations algéro-nigériennes ont toujours été empreintes de compréhension, d’entente et de coopération, malgré une période inhabituelle de froid, dont les malentendus ont été vite dissipés par les hautes autorités des deux pays. Celles-ci affichent aujourd’hui une sérénité et une ferme volonté d’approfondir les liens historiques et fraternels qui unissent les deux peuples afin de faire de la stabilité du Sahel un levier de développement économique commun. Une évolution importante de la doctrine algérienne Dans ce contexte, la décision de l'Algérie d'envoyer un contingent militaire au Niger marque une évolution importante de sa doctrine. La motivation affichée est d'abord sécuritaire : lutter contre les menaces transfrontalières et protéger la stabilité de la zone sahélo-saharienne. Il faut rappeler que cette zone est soumise régulièrement à des menaces, car largement exposée à la contrebande, au trafic de drogues et aux groupes armés, et que la frontière libyenne est devenue, par la force des choses, un point de vigilance majeur, et ce, depuis 2011. D’autant plus que la sécurité régionale est un pilier central de la politique étrangère algérienne, grâce à une approche globale (diplomatique, sécuritaire, politique et économique) permettant d’œuvrer notamment pour un Sahel stable. Aussi, sur le plan économique, plusieurs projets stratégiques constituent un puissant moteur de rapprochement entre l’Algérie et le Niger. Il s’agit de la coopération dans le secteur énergétique, notamment à travers les investissements de Sonatrach et de Sonelgaz. C’est aussi le projet de gazoduc transsaharien Nigeria-Niger-Algérie (TSGP), destiné à acheminer le gaz nigérian vers l'Europe, ainsi que des infrastructures de transport et de télécommunications, dont les projets de fibre optique et la route transsaharienne. Autrement dit, l'Algérie et le Niger cherchent clairement à bâtir un partenariat stratégique combinant sécurité, énergie, infrastructures et commerce, avec l'ambition de faire du Sahel un espace plus sûr et porteur de développement durable. L’Algérie change de stratégie au Sahel La vision algéro-nigérienne semble aujourd'hui plus large, car elle cherche à sécuriser plusieurs axes simultanément de sorte à protéger un futur réseau de connectivité continentale susceptible de faire de l'axe Algérie-Niger-Nigeria-Tchad l'un des principaux corridors économiques africains dans le cadre de la zone de libre-échange du continent africain (ZLECAf). La sécurisation du Sahel, du moins de la zone algéro-nigérienne, dépasse largement la seule protection du projet de gazoduc transsaharien. Elle conditionne potentiellement la viabilité d'un vaste corridor commercial continental avec la mise en œuvre des mécanismes de la ZLECAf. En définitive, on assiste au passage progressif de l’Algérie d’une logique de défense de ses frontières à une logique de sécurisation de son environnement régional immédiat, lorsque celui-ci touche directement à ses intérêts économiques et stratégiques. items.title: Pour sauver la biodiversité, il faut repenser la liberté
items.description: Testez le Grand Continent . Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois « Il ne peut y avoir aucun abaissement de l’ambition convenue. » C’est l’annonce qu’a faite le ministre d’État irlandais Christopher O’Sullivan au nom de la présidence du Conseil lorsqu’il a présenté le 12 octobre la position que l’Union européenne défendra à Erevan, où se tient depuis le 19 octobre la dix-septième conférence des parties à la Convention sur la diversité biologique Multilatéralisme : le Conseil arrête la position de l’UE en vue des sommets sur le changement climatique et la biodiversité », communiqué de presse, 12 octobre 2026.'> 4 . Si l’Union peut se permettre ce ton, c’est parce qu’elle fait figure de bonne élève. Le cadre mondial adopté à la COP15 en 2022 fixe l’objectif de protéger 30 % des terres et des mers d’ici 2030 et l’Union avait atteint, fin 2022, 26,1 % de ses terres et 12,3 % de ses mers, quand la moyenne mondiale plafonne respectivement à 18,4 et 10 % UN Biodiversity Conference 2026 : COP17 in a nutshell », 2026.'> 5 . Cette posture de leader contraste toutefois avec certaines décisions européennes prises au cours des deux dernières années. Par exemple, elle a doublé, passant de 5 à 10 %, le recul des prairies permanentes que la politique agricole commune tolère avant d’obliger les États à agir. Le loup, lui, a été retiré de la liste des espèces strictement protégées, une première pour une espèce bénéficiant de ce statut en droit européen. Les directives Habitats et Oiseaux, qui fondent depuis plus de trente ans la politique européenne de la nature, sont soumises désormais à un « test de résistance », par lequel la Commission veut vérifier qu’elles atteignent leurs objectifs à moindre coût et réduire la « charge administrative inutile » qu’elles imposeraient. Enfin, l’application du règlement contre la déforestation importée a été reportée pour la deuxième fois, et le devoir de vigilance comme les obligations de reporting de durabilité des entreprises ont été allégés Vagues de déréglementation sur l’environnement et la santé en Europe , juillet 2026 : paquet « Omnibus III » sur la politique agricole commune (décembre 2025) ; modification du statut de protection du loup (entrée en vigueur le 14 juillet 2025) ; second report du règlement sur la déforestation importée (vote du Parlement européen du 26 novembre 2025) ; paquet « Omnibus I » sur les directives CSRD et CSDDD (décembre 2025). Commission européenne, « Commission seeks public opinion on how EU Nature Directives are working », 12 mai 2026 (test de résistance annoncé en décembre 2025, consultation close le 10 août 2026).'> 6 . Le meilleur élève de la COP biodiversité desserre visiblement ses propres législations. Mais ce paradoxe en dit moins sur l’Europe que sur la COP elle-même. Pour le comprendre, regardons de plus près ce qu’est une COP biodiversité. Une architecture empruntée au climat Dans l’arène publique, le terme de COP est avant tout associé aux questions climatiques. On parle très peu de la COP biodiversité, et le cas échéant, elle reste cantonnée au statut de petite sœur de la COP climat. Car bien que les deux conventions aient vu le jour ensemble au sommet de la Terre de Rio en juin 1992, le climat a construit ses institutions le premier, et la biodiversité a emprunté le chemin qu’il avait tracé. Ce mimétisme se retrouve dans la Plateforme intergouvernementale scientifique et politique sur la biodiversité et les services écosystémiques (IPBES) qui a été créée en 2012 sur le modèle du Groupe d’experts intergouvernemental sur l’évolution du climat (GIEC). De même, le cadre mondial adopté à Kunming-Montréal en décembre 2022, qui fixe vingt-trois cibles pour 2030, a été salué comme le « moment Paris » de la biodiversité, en référence à l’accord de Paris de 2015 car chaque COP s’est dotée de son chiffre-étalon, 1,5 °C pour le climat, 30 % des terres et des mers protégées en 2030 pour la biodiversité, objectif aussitôt baptisé « 30×30 ». Depuis juillet 2025, la Commission européenne propose également des « crédits nature » conçus sur le modèle des crédits carbone Feuille de route vers les crédits « Nature » , 7 juillet 2025.'> 7 . Et aujourd’hui, la COP d’Erevan doit produire la revue mondiale du cadre de Kunming-Montréal qui n’est rien d’autre que le pendant du premier bilan mondial du climat dressé à Dubaï en 2023. La liberté est au cœur du débat écologique, et étonnamment les doctrines contemporaines qui y contribuent l’ont contournée plutôt qu’affrontée. Lauriane Mouysset Toutefois, les réunions préparatoires à cette revue mondiale, qui se sont tenues cet été à Nairobi, ont conclu que, sans accélération rapide, aucune des vingt-trois cibles du cadre ne sera atteinte en 2030 Summary, conclusions and key messages of the global review of collective progress in the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework », 22 juillet 2026, examiné à Nairobi (SBSTTA-28 et SBI-7, juillet-août 2026).'> 8 . Mais ce constat d’échec n’est pas inédit car le cadre précédent avait connu le même sort : en 2020, aucune des vingt cibles d’Aichi, fixées en 2010 pour la décennie, n’avait été pleinement atteinte Perspectives mondiales de la diversité biologique 5 , septembre 2020.'> 9 . Deux cadres successifs, portés par des gouvernements différents et adossés à des cibles différentes, aboutissant au même résultat, invitent à réfléchir à ce qu’ils ont en commun et à ce qui pourrait être responsable de ces échecs, au-delà des problèmes classiques de budget ou de lobbies. Leur dénominateur commun, c’est cet héritage, tiré des institutions climatiques et de leur logique bien particulière, celle de l’agrégation : un objet unique, mesuré partout dans la même unité, qui permet d’établir des comptes nationaux chiffrés, de comparer les trajectoires des pays, puis de mesurer leur écart à des cibles fixées d’avance. Rien ne garantit qu’un tel système fonctionne pour la biodiversité. Une convention lucide sur la biodiversité Si le climat n’a pas livré tous ses secrets, sa science est aujourd’hui assez établie pour raisonner en probabilités : le GIEC juge « sans équivoque » l’influence humaine sur le réchauffement, et estime qu’un doublement de la concentration de dioxyde de carbone réchaufferait probablement la planète de 2,5 à 4 °C Changement climatique 2021 : les bases scientifiques physiques, contribution du groupe de travail I au sixième rapport d’évaluation, résumé à l’intention des décideurs , 2021.'> 10 . Pour la biodiversité, la connaissance est plus parcellaire. Environ 2 millions d’espèces ont été décrites « How many species are there ? » , Our World in Data , avril 2026.'> 11 , sur un total estimé à quelque 8,7 millions « How Many Species Are There on Earth and in the Ocean ? » , PLoS Biology, 9(8), 2011.'> 12 . Ce savoir est de surcroît inégal : les mammifères sont bien inventoriés, les micro-organismes beaucoup moins. De même, les milieux terrestres sont mieux étudiés que les abysses océaniques. La Convention sur la diversité biologique a reconnu cette spécificité dès son préambule, en 1992, en posant que, face à une menace sensible, l’absence de certitude scientifique totale ne doit pas servir de prétexte pour différer les mesures Préambule de la Convention sur la diversité biologique , Rio de Janeiro, 1992.'> 13 . Mais loin de n’être qu’une question pour les scientifiques, les deux faces de la crise écologique diffèrent aussi par la place qu’y occupe la société. La crise climatique est avant tout planétaire : une tonne de carbone émise à Lyon pèse sur le climat autant qu’une tonne émise à Shanghai. Ce qui compte pour le climat, c’est la quantité de tonnes émises au total et ce qui compte dans les négociations, c’est la coordination de la réduction des émissions puis, depuis la COP de Charm el-Cheikh en 2022, la création d’un fonds pour les pertes et préjudices subis par des pays peu responsables du réchauffement 14 . Rien d’étonnant à ce que la question climatique soit longtemps restée confinée à des sphères expertes et diplomatiques, les entreprises et les ménages n’étant convoqués que de manière descendante pour orienter leur comportement grâce à des instruments économiques ou législatifs. Le meilleur élève de la COP biodiversité desserre visiblement ses propres législations. Mais ce paradoxe en dit moins sur l’Europe que sur la COP elle-même. Lauriane Mouysset Mais cette équivalence des tonnes de carbone ne fonctionne pas pour la biodiversité. Une prairie retournée dans le Cantal ne se compense pas par une forêt protégée en Laponie, parce que les espèces et les relations qui disparaissent avec elle ne se trouvent pas là-bas. La crise de la biodiversité est une question locale avant d’être internationale. Et depuis 2000, les textes de la Convention ont bien pris acte de cette inversion d’échelle grâce à l’approche écosystémique. Son premier principe affirme que les objectifs de gestion des terres, des eaux et des ressources biologiques relèvent d’un choix de société quand le deuxième précise qu’il faut décentraliser la gestion au niveau approprié le plus bas et le douzième qu’il faut associer tous les secteurs concernés de la société 15 . En 2024, à Cali, la Convention a poursuivi dans cette voie en créant un organe subsidiaire permanent consacré aux peuples autochtones et aux communautés locales Décision 16/5 : création d’un organe subsidiaire sur l’article 8 j) de la Convention , Cali, 2024.'> 16 . Enfin, se pose la question de la valeur. La molécule de dioxyde de carbone pèse lourdement sur les sociétés humaines et leurs économies, mais presque personne ne lui accorde de considération morale : limiter le réchauffement reste d’abord une nécessité matérielle. Il en va autrement de la biodiversité, et là encore la Convention l’a écrit dès 1992, dans la toute première phrase de son préambule, qui s’ouvre sur la « valeur intrinsèque » de la diversité biologique avant d’énumérer notamment ses valeurs écologiques, économiques, sociales, culturelles et esthétiques Préambule de la Convention sur la diversité biologique , Rio de Janeiro, 1992.'> 17 . Les trente années suivantes ont élargi les raisons pour lesquelles il faudrait protéger la biodiversité : en 2005 avec les services que les écosystèmes rendent aux sociétés, avec l’Évaluation des écosystèmes pour le millénaire ; en 2010 avec leur poids économique et l’étude internationale The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity (TEEB) ; en 2019 avec l’urgence scientifique, avec l’évaluation mondiale de l’IPBES qui estimait qu’un million d’espèces étaient menacées d’extinction ; jusqu’à assumer en 2022 un pluralisme des valeurs et des visions du monde, consacré par l’IPBES et repris dans le cadre de Kunming-Montréal Rapport d’évaluation mondiale de la biodiversité et des services écosystémiques, résumé à l’intention des décideurs , 2019 ; IPBES, Évaluation méthodologique des diverses valeurs et de l’évaluation de la nature, 2022 ; Cadre mondial de la biodiversité de Kunming-Montréal, décision 15/4, 2022.'> 18 . Mais si l’institution connaît et reconnaît ces spécificités, pourquoi le cadre qu’elle a bâti continue-t-il de traiter la biodiversité comme du carbone ? Le tabou du renoncement La réponse se trouve dans le rôle que la COP s’assigne. Elle veut fédérer des États souverains autour d’un cadre commun en énonçant des ambitions sans coercition, c’est-à-dire sans contraindre bien sûr, mais sans évoquer non plus ce à quoi il faudra renoncer pour les atteindre. Parce que nommer les renoncements reviendrait à prendre le risque de braquer ceux qui devraient les consentir. Les COP climat ont suivi cette ligne pendant près de trente ans. Il a fallu attendre la vingt-huitième, à Dubaï en 2023, pour qu’une décision appelle à « s’éloigner des combustibles fossiles » dans les systèmes énergétiques : enfin a été nommé ce à quoi il faudrait renoncer pour faire avancer la transition énergétique et climatique 19 . Toutefois, cette ligne n’a jamais empêché de fixer une cible climatique mondiale parce que l’équation du climat est simple : une tonne évitée ici vaut une tonne évitée ailleurs, une énergie peut en remplacer une autre, si bien que l’objectif pouvait être arrêté sans expliciter le renoncement lui-même. La valeur la plus structurante de nos sociétés se trouve ainsi aujourd’hui abandonnée toute entière à ceux qui ne travaillent que contre la transition écologique. Lauriane Mouysset La biodiversité n’a pas ce luxe. Le cadre mondial de la biodiversité n’existe qu’à travers des milliers de cibles locales : il ne peut donc faire l’impasse ni sur la connaissance partielle des écosystèmes sur chacun des territoires ni sur les visions du monde des parties prenantes qui y sont mises en jeu. Pour les énoncer, il faut faire des choix sur nos incertitudes et arbitrer au sein de nos systèmes de valeurs. L’équation est complexe et la résoudre requiert d’expliciter les renoncements en jeu, leur périmètre et ce qu’ils engagent. C’est précisément sur ce point que se verrouille la COP biodiversité : elle voudrait accomplir le premier geste, énoncer le cadre mondial, sans passer par le second, expliciter les renoncements, qui en est pourtant la condition. L’identification de ce verrou éclaire le paradoxe européen évoqué en introduction. L’Europe est bonne élève précisément là où il n’y a plus rien à arbitrer : dans une aire protégée, le renoncement est consenti au moment du classement et n’a plus à être rejoué. Dans le même temps, l’Europe desserre ses exigences dès que les renoncements sont négociables : la prairie, la forêt ou la chaîne d’approvisionnement d’une entreprise impliquent une biodiversité ordinaire dans laquelle la question de ce qu’on laisse s’éteindre au profit de ce qui sera préservé, en fonction de ce que l’on sait et de ce que l’on valorise, n’est jamais vraiment close. La COP biodiversité est ainsi prisonnière d’un tabou, celui du renoncement et de ce qui le justifie. Et ce tabou est d’autant plus pernicieux que la Convention mentionne explicitement la question des valeurs, donnant ainsi le sentiment qu’elles sont considérées. Mais reconnaître la pluralité des valeurs n’est pas suffisant pour organiser leur arbitrage. L’évaluation de l’IPBES place les valeurs côte à côte et demande qu’aucune ne soit ignorée, sans jamais dire laquelle doit céder quand elles se heurtent. Un cadre qui reconnaît le pluralisme sans organiser l’arbitrage laisse le renoncement se décider ailleurs, dans les rapports de force, au gré des calendriers électoraux et des paquets de simplification. Pour lever ce tabou, il faut identifier, lorsque le renoncement se décide ailleurs, au nom de quoi il est refusé. La liberté dont personne ne parle Les textes européens parlent de « simplification » ou de « compétitivité », mais ces mots ne défendent rien de moins qu’une liberté. Car dans les démocraties libérales, tout renoncement est ultimement perçu comme une perte de liberté. Limiter le retournement des prairies touche à la liberté d’exploiter sa terre comme on l’entend. Maintenir la protection stricte du loup, à celle d’exercer un métier, celui d’éleveur en montagne, sans en supporter seul le coût. Exclure du marché les produits issus de la déforestation, c’est toucher à la liberté de commercer. Exiger des entreprises qu’elles rendent compte de leurs atteintes à l’environnement le long de leurs chaînes d’approvisionnement, c’est toucher à celle d’entreprendre. Préserver les habitats et les oiseaux, c’est toucher à la liberté d’aménager. La liberté est la valeur qui rassemble le plus en France. Le Baromètre de la République réalisé par Ipsos en juillet 2026 la place en tête des trois termes de la devise : 96 % des personnes interrogées la jugent importante, dont 74 % très importante, devant la fraternité (91 %) et l’égalité (90 %). Elle est surtout la seule des trois dont l’importance ne varie pas avec la proximité politique Baromètre de la République, deuxième vague, enquête réalisée du 15 au 17 juillet 2026 auprès de 1 001 personnes .'> 20 . C’est donc sans surprise que les exigences sur la biodiversité sont lues comme des contraintes, comme des restrictions de liberté. Mais puisqu’avancer face à la crise de la biodiversité ne peut s’imposer par le haut et puisque nous avons besoin d’embarquer la société pour qu’une meilleure réalité écologique advienne, cette position hégémonique de la liberté ne gagnerait-elle pas à être vue comme une opportunité ? Si la Convention a raison d’expliciter le pluralisme de valeurs pour fédérer les visions du monde, pourquoi ne commencerait-elle pas sa réflexion sur l’arbitrage des valeurs par celle qui est à la fois la plus fédératrice et la raison du recul des législations ? La liberté est au cœur du débat écologique, et étonnamment les doctrines contemporaines qui y contribuent l’ont contournée plutôt qu’affrontée : chacune a placé une valeur à côté d’elle sans jamais la redéfinir. Citons en guise d’exemple l’écologie de guerre qui adosse la transition énergétique à la puissance, la sécurité écologique à une « abondance nouvelle » ou encore l’internationalisme écosocialiste aux besoins. La valeur la plus structurante de nos sociétés se trouve ainsi aujourd’hui abandonnée toute entière à ceux qui ne travaillent que contre la transition écologique. Washington le dit désormais sans détour, comme dans le décret présidentiel du 20 janvier 2025 où la levée des contraintes environnementales est présentée comme une « libération » de l’énergie américaine « Unleashing American Energy » , 20 janvier 2025.'> 21 . Plus que jamais, la COP biodiversité, et plus largement les intellectuels de la transition écologique, doivent formuler les arbitrages dans la langue de la liberté, sans quoi les ambitions céderont dès qu’on les attaquera dans cette langue. Un cadre qui reconnaît le pluralisme sans organiser l’arbitrage laisse le renoncement se décider ailleurs, dans les rapports de force, au gré des calendriers électoraux et des paquets de simplification. Lauriane Mouysset La difficulté vient de la manière dont nous pensons inconsciemment le renoncement. Influencés par une certaine lecture des Lumières, nous le pensons comme une amputation de la liberté, comme l’absence d’entraves. Or nos libertés de produire, de commercer ou d’aménager reposent sur des équilibres écologiques que nous connaissons mal et que nous ne contrôlons pas. Chacune de nos décisions sollicite certains de ces équilibres et en épargne d’autres : qu’on le veuille ou non, nous choisissons déjà, mais sans le savoir et sans l’avoir décidé ensemble. L’éthique de la viabilité étayée de la théorie mathématique du même nom permet de rendre ce choix explicite. Plutôt que de chercher la meilleure trajectoire, elle délimite l’ensemble des décisions qui maintiennent dans la durée les conditions écologiques, économiques et sociales d’une société Viability Theory , Birkhäuser, 1991 ; Lauriane Mouysset, La liberté des limites , Éditions de l’Observatoire, 2026.'> 22 . Mais déterminer ces conditions ne relève pas de l’expertise scientifique, puisqu’il s’agit de décider ce que l’on refuse de perdre : ce tracé revient aux citoyens, éclairés par la science. L’espace viable y gagne alors à la fois en lucidité, parce qu’il s’appuie sur ce que l’on sait des écosystèmes et de leurs dynamiques, et en légitimité, parce qu’il procède d’une décision collective. Et c’est précisément cette double exigence qui fait de la limite une liberté : être libre, ce n’est pas ignorer les limites, c’est définir ensemble, en connaissance de cause, l’espace viable dans lequel on évolue et les limites qui le constituent. Dans cette perspective, le renoncement cesse d’être une contrainte imposée de l’extérieur, il devient constitutif de la liberté, et l’ambition écologique avec lui. C’est au fond le choix de société qu’appelait déjà le premier principe de l’approche écosystémique, doté enfin d’un cadre éthique. Ce chantier pourrait revenir à l’Europe, héritière de la tradition libérale, au moment où les États-Unis, qui n’ont jamais ratifié la Convention et ont quitté l’IPBES en janvier, brandissent la liberté contre l’écologie 23 . Si elle s’en saisit, la liberté pourrait enfin cesser d’être l’autel sur lequel la COP biodiversité sacrifie ses ambitions, pour en devenir plutôt le fondement. L’article Pour sauver la biodiversité, il faut repenser la liberté est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

4 students, one lady killed in Niger governor’s convoy road crash
items.description: By Clare Nnabuike, Minna Five person, four male students and a young lady have died in a fatal accident involving the Niger state governor Mohammed Umaru Bago’s convoy in Minna, the state capital. The incident happened on Monday at Gidan Mangoro community along the Minna–Bida Road. It followed a head-on collision between a high speeding Hilux van in the convoy of Bago, and a private Peugeot 206 car. The lady identified as Mrs Nafisa was driving the car and died at the spot of the accident. She was said to be a staff of an NGO, and Programme Manager at Labspace, and the Founder of Wosh Mart Service Ltd. A resident of Gidan Mangoro, Abdullahi Musa, told Vanguard that the accident occurred at about 11:35am when the governor was returning from Bida. He and his team paid a condolence visit on the Etsu Nupe and chairman of the Niger state council of traditional rulers Alhaji Yahaya Abubakar over the passage of the Sagi Nupe Hajia Aisha. He said the occupants of the private car driven by Nafisa were suspected to be postgraduate students of the Federal University of Technology, Minna. His words, “The people in the private car died instantly, while those in the government Hilux sustained serious injuries with the driver dying on the spot. Nafisa “The accident was caused by wrongful overtaking by the Hilux in the governor’s convoy. The other car was in its lane when the Hilux rammed into it.” A member of staff of Minna General Hospital, where the victims were rushed to told Vanguard that three people died on the spot while two other people died due to high level of injuries sustain from the crash. “Some of the injured victims were subsequently referred to IBB Specialist Hospital for advanced medical care,” he said. Vanguard gathered that one of the occupants of the Hilux van was a former Niger state local government council chairman who sustained fractures to his legs but was still alive at the time of this report. The Niger State Sector Commander of the Federal Road Safety Corps, FRSC Aishat Sa’adu, confirmed the road crash but said that by the time her officers arrived at the scene, the victims had already been evacuated to the hospital. The Police Public Relations Officer of the Niger state command Superintendent of Police Wasiu Abiodun confirmed the incident and said the accident was under investigation. He did not however give the names or numbers of the deceased. “The accident occured this morning and we are investigating it,” Abiodun said. The post 4 students, one lady killed in Niger governor’s convoy road crash appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: State Police: Presidency seeks private sector support for funding, blueprint
items.description: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA—THE Presidency has challenged Nigeria’s organised private sector to develop a comprehensive financing and implementation blueprint for the proposed state police system, saying that businesses must take an active role in building the security institutions required to protect investments, create jobs and strengthen economic resilience. Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, Mr. Femi Gbajabiamila, who made the challenge, tasked the Nigerian Economic Summit Group, NESG, chambers of commerce and business associations with producing practical proposals for financing, institutional management and accountable partnerships to support the decentralisation of policing. Speaking during a plenary session on “Security, Stability and Economic Resilience” at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit, in Abuja, on Monday, Gbajabiamila said President Bola Tinubu’s commitment to establishing state police presented an opportunity for businesses to contribute directly to the development of security institutions capable of supporting sustainable economic growth. According to him: “I, therefore, ask the Nigerian Economic Summit Group to carry this engagement beyond our meeting. Bring forward a considered private sector contribution on financing and implementing state police, with practical proposals for accountable partnerships. ”Take that work into the legislative process and into your engagement with state governments. For our part, we remain answerable for turning reform into protection that people can rely on,” he said. Gbajabiamila urged business leaders to engage governors and legislators on the proposed reform, drawing attention to the relationship between effective local policing, employment generation and investment decisions. ”Your participation should also improve the substance of the reform. As the legislative process proceeds, examine the proposals for financing and oversight. Bring your experience of managing institutions and controlling expenditure to that discussion. Help us understand the security failures that prevent viable projects from proceeding,” he stated. He, however cautioned that private sector involvement must be transparent and should never compromise the independence of police institutions. ”Where businesses provide resources, those contributions need published accounts and independent scrutiny.‎ ‎”Public funding must remain dependable, and a donation must never purchase influence over an investigation or preferential treatment. The object is to strengthen a public service on which every citizen can rely,” he warned.‎ ‎He said providing vehicles, uniforms and other equipment at the commencement of operations would be insufficient without sustainable arrangements for personnel salaries, professional training and operational maintenance. ‎”Financial readiness is equally important. A state taking on policing must be able to sustain the service after the initial purchase of vehicles and uniforms.‎ ‎”Regular pay and continued training are essential to professional conduct. An institution that cannot meet its obligations to its officers becomes vulnerable to private patrons and unlawful demands on the public,” he cautioned.‎ He assured that federal policing would continue in states not yet financially or institutionally prepared to establish their own police services.‎ ‎Providing an update on the legislative process, Gbajabiamila confirmed that 24 State Houses of Assembly had approved the constitutional amendment providing for state police as of October 23, meeting the required two-thirds threshold.‎ ‎He disclosed that the Presidential Working Group had submitted the draft National Policing Bill and 29 consequential amendment bills to the Federal Ministry of Justice on October 19 for legislative review. The United States Mission in Nigeria has announced a major breakthrough in the fight against transnational cybercrime, with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, FBI, arresting nine suspects in Nigeria in an operation targeting scam centres stealing billions of dollars from Americans. FBI Director, Kash Patel, disclosed this in a post on X which was reposted by the US Mission in Nigeria, saying the operation, code-named Operation Blackout, is taking the fight directly to international cybercriminal networks. According to Patel, the Nigeria operation delivered nine arrests, seizure of 53 electronic devices and identification of $11 million in potentially freezable funds across multiple countries. “Operation Blackout is taking the fight directly to the international cybercriminal networks stealing billions from Americans,” Patel said. “These scam centers exploit innocent victims, steal life savings, and operate across international borders believing they are beyond the reach of law enforcement. They’re wrong,” he stated. He commended Nigerian law enforcement and partners in London for their cooperation. “Thanks to Nigerian law enforcement and our partners in London for their outstanding cooperation,” Patel said, warning: “To the criminals targeting Americans from overseas: Justice will fibd you.” While the FBI did not name the Nigerian agency involved or the locations of the arrests, the operation is part of a wider international enforcement exercise coordinated from London. According to the US Department of Justice, the broader crackdown resulted in 28 arrests across Nigeria and Ghana and the seizure of hundreds of electronic devices. The operation also involved Meta and 14 other technology companies, leading to the removal of more than 3.7 million fraudulent accounts, pages and groups linked to West African scam networks. Reports indicate that 19 of the arrests were made in Ghana, where 117 victims, said to have been trafficked and forced to work in a residential compound running scam operations, are pending repatriation to Nigeria. The arrests come amid heightened US-Nigeria cooperation on cybercrime. In September, South African authorities handed over six Nigerians to FBI officials over allegations of defrauding more than 100 women in a romance scam scheme. In August, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, extradited two Nigerians to the US over alleged online sexual exploitation and sextortion of two teenage boys who later died by suicide. In August 2025, the FBI arrested 22 Nigerians for alleged involvement in financially motivated sextortion schemes linked to a rise in suicides among American teenagers. The FBI said Nigerian authorities will prosecute the nine suspects arrested in the latest operation for violations of Nigerian law, while investigations continue to freeze the $11 million identified across several countries. items.title: Cenpower clears 600 tonnes of waste from Sega Beach
items.description: Cenpower Generation Ltd says it removed 600 tonnes of waste from Sega Beach during the fourth edition of its annual KIPP Clean Project, highlighting the scale of shoreline pollution. The exercise brought together employees, Kpone residents, the Kpone Katamanso Municipal Assembly, and waste management partners to clean the beach in the Tema Industrial enclave. Cenpower, which owns the Kpone Independent Power Plant (KIPP), launched the project in September 2023 to tackle coastal pollution, protect marine ecosystems and encourage responsible waste disposal. This year’s exercise involved Cenpower Operations (Cenops) and Excelior Solution Services, which supported shoreline cleaning, waste collection, sorting and safe disposal. Cenpower’s Chief Executive, Theophilus Sackey, said protecting the environment required collective action beyond individual businesses’ operations. He warned that waste dumped into the ocean could wash back onto beaches, creating recurring pollution problems for coastal communities. He called for clean-up exercises to be supported by responsible disposal practices and sustained public participation. The Director of Environmental Services at the Kpone Katamanso Municipal Assembly, Freeman George, commended Cenpower for maintaining the initiative. Speaking on behalf of the Municipal Chief Executive, he urged businesses, institutions, and residents to help keep the municipality clean. He stressed that lasting improvements would depend on changes in everyday waste disposal habits. He said environmental cleanliness should be a daily responsibility rather than an activity reserved for organised clean-up exercises. Community members welcomed the initiative and called for continued collaboration to prevent waste from accumulating along the shoreline. Cenops Plant Manager Darlington Ahuble said employee participation helped reinforce environmental awareness and responsible practices. He explained that environmental compliance and cleanliness formed part of the company’s operational responsibilities. He urged employees, partners and neighbouring communities to sustain those efforts beyond the annual exercise. Cenpower’s Director of Legal and Corporate Affairs, Elizabeth Akin-Taylor, also called for greater community involvement in coastal protection. She said local participation could strengthen ownership of environmental initiatives and encourage residents to prevent littering. According to her, the project’s value extended beyond the volume of waste collected. It also offered an opportunity to promote responsible environmental practices and strengthen cooperation among stakeholders. The initiative aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 14, which focuses on conserving oceans, seas and marine resources.
