items.title: Trump’s Cheesecake Factory Dissent
items.description: The Republican Party, with one notable exception, has settled on a populist closing message: Barack Obama’s weekend joke that the president has “got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory” represents a grave insult to middle-class Americans. Alas, the sole Republican who appears unable to cooperate with this message is Donald Trump. In reality, Obama’s crack was mainly aimed at the gaudy aesthetic shared by Trump and the former Iraqi dictator. And even if the joke had not mentioned Saddam, it is hardly a swipe at the Cheesecake Factory to suggest that its campy decor, while perfectly suitable as a backdrop for a family munching on a plate of fried macaroni and cheese, is an inappropriate sensibility for the Oval Office. And even if Obama had committed a genuine gaffe, it seems odd for Republicans to try to make the election about an opponent who is (1) not on the ballot and (2) the most popular living politician in America. But when your party has presided over rising inflation and a failed war of choice, the messaging options aren’t great. And this pseudo-scandal does have the benefit of helping Republicans change the subject from Trump’s obsession with gilding the White House to Democratic elitism. So various GOP mouthpieces have come forward to express their indignation on behalf of the salt-of-the-earth Cheesecake Factory diners that Obama had so viciously slandered. “It goes exactly to why Democrats lost the middle class, why they lost blue-collar voters. Because it’s kind of a guns-and-religion-clinging kind of comment, and it turns a lot of people in this country off,” explained Fox News’s Martha MacCallum . “To all of those diners in Cleveland, Grand Rapids, and beyond, here’s Mr. Obama’s message: How déclassé,” editorialized The Wall Street Journal . Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , not to be outdone, appeared in front of a Cheesecake Factory and told reporters, “I would tell the Martha’s Vineyard set to give it a try,” as if Obama had criticized the restaurant’s food. [ Read: Leave the Cheesecake Factory out of this ] This posturing is part of a familiar ritual in American politics. Our candidate was born in a humble log cabin and has the backing of the common people, whereas your candidate is the son of privilege and represents the aristocracy . Because he is instinctively elitist, however, Trump has always struggled with the populist script. After being elected as the leader of what pundits depicted as a populist uprising, he would sometimes bristle at the notion that his enemies constituted an elite. “Why are they elite?” he said during his first term. “I have a much better apartment than they do. I’m smarter than they are. I’m richer than they are. I became president, and they didn’t.” He would tell his supporters at rallies, “You are the elite. They’re not the elite.” Trump seems to have an especially difficult time feigning populism when the target is Black. Asked by a reporter at the White House gaggle about Obama’s gibe, Trump attacked Obama as low-class and dumb. “He doesn’t notice dirt and filth that hadn’t been cleaned, where the walls hadn’t been cleaned for years,” Trump said. “We have to explain that to Obama because he doesn’t understand it, because he’s not a smart guy.” Attacking Obama as an out-of-touch coastal elitist, rather than a slum-dweller who dirtied up a pristine home, is a concept that Trump’s mind is apparently too racist to process. Nor could Trump bring himself to pretend to think that the humble White House would be lucky to have decor as luxurious and dignified as the inside of a Cheesecake Factory, the veritable temple of the middle class. Instead, he delivered a 500-word monologue about the palatial renovations he had overseen. [ Read: The rush-job presidency ] “I fixed it with the finest artisans in the world,” he said. “I’ve reskinned the building beautifully with the highest, most talented people. Anywhere in the world, you’re not going to find more talent.” If Trump’s allies were trying to dispel the impression that the president was overly focused on improving his own residence at the expense of his other duties, Trump appeared eager to confirm it. Indeed, he emphasized the great time and expense the work had consumed. At a rally last night, Trump returned to Obama’s Cheesecake slander, while characteristically proceeding to substantiate the gist of it. “He was very critical of me, because I spend time,” he told the crowd. He then spent several minutes walking through the renovations in tedious detail—confirming, rather than rebutting, the impression that he is obsessed with the project. He repeated his boast that he employed “the best artisans you’ve ever seen.” And he complained that the building he inherited contained materials that looked as if they came from a store that sold home items to hardworking, ordinary Americans. “We took tile that was broken, that was—I mean, I don’t want to say from Home Depot, but it does come from a box, and it’s not for the White House.” Not only did Trump once again fail to assail Obama as a snob and pose as the champion of the Cheesecake proletariat, but he went in the opposite direction. He dismissed Obama as such a rube that he would settle for appointing the White House with tile that could have come from a store as low-class as Home Depot .

items.title: La coalition de l’opposition démocratique condamne la répression de la manifestation des étudiants hier lundi
items.description: Le chef de file de la coalition de l'opposition démocratique en Mauritanie a condamné ce qu'il a qualifié de répression contre les étudiants et l'intervention violente des forces de sécurité lors de leurs manifestations, appelant à mettre fin aux restrictions des libertés publiques et à ouvrir un dialogue sérieux avec les représentants des étudiants. Dans un communiqué publié ce mardi, le chef de file a déclaré que le recours à la force contre les étudiants était contraire aux principes de l’État de droit et au respect des libertés publiques et des droits fondamentaux des citoyens. Le communiqué a réaffirmé que la manifestation pacifique et la liberté d’expression constituaient un droit constitutionnel, exigeant que les droits légaux des étudiants soient respectés et que leur droit de manifester soit garanti sans menace ni intimidation. La coalition a appelé à répondre aux revendications des étudiants par des solutions concrètes, loin d’une approche sécuritaire, et a exprimé sa solidarité avec les personnes touchées par ces événements. Elle a souligné que la stabilité du pays passe par le respect de la loi, la préservation des libertés et l’affirmation de la justice, et non par la répression des voix qui revendiquent leurs droits. Lundi, les environs de l’université de Nouakchott ont été le théâtre de manifestations étudiantes réclamant la mise en place de transports publics. La police est intervenue pour disperser les manifestants, tandis que les syndicats étudiants appelaient à l’ouverture d’un dialogue et au respect du droit à la liberté d’expression pacifique.

items.title: Qu’est-ce que la géopolitique ?
items.description: Qu’est-ce que la « géopolitique » ? Dans un contexte mondial où les enjeux internationaux occupent une place de plus en plus importante, l’usage du terme « géopolitique » s’est de plus en plus répandu dans le débat public au cours des dernières décennies. items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : plus de 600 professionnels de santé et 30 ambulances mobilisés
items.description: Le ministère de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique a mobilisé plus de 600 professionnels de santé et 30 ambulances, avec une réserve, pour assurer la couverture sanitaire des Jeux olympiques de la Jeunesse (Joj) Dakar 2026. Ce dispositif a fait l’objet, mardi, d’une visite de terrain à Diamniadio, à l’Aéroport international Blaise Diagne (Aibd) et à Mbour, en vue d’apprécier le niveau de préparation des équipes et de vérifier la disponibilité des moyens déployés. Le dispositif sanitaire repose sur une organisation coordonnée entre les postes médicaux installés sur les sites de compétition, les services d’urgence, les ambulances et les structures hospitalières de référence. Les professionnels de santé mobilisés seront répartis entre les différents sites, les équipes d’intervention et les établissements de prise en charge. L’Hôpital d’Enfants de Diamniadio (HED), désigné comme hôpital officiel des JOJ, bénéficie d’un renforcement de son plateau technique. Selon le dossier de presse du ministère, l’ensemble des équipements prévus sont disponibles pour améliorer les capacités de diagnostic, de surveillance et de prise en charge des patients nécessitant des soins spécialisés. L’Établissement public de santé de Mbour a également fait l’objet de travaux de mise aux normes. La prévention des risques sanitaires constitue un autre volet du dispositif. La surveillance épidémiologique est renforcée, notamment aux postes frontières et aux points d’entrée. Des bulletins épidémiologiques sont régulièrement partagés et les équipes médicales des délégations et des fédérations ont été sensibilisées au système national de veille. Des exercices de simulation ont également été organisés à l’Hôpital d’Enfants de Diamniadio, dont une simulation grandeur nature. En parallèle, la Pharmacie nationale d’approvisionnement (SEN-PNA) assure la distribution des médicaments et des consommables médicaux sur les sites. Le ministère prévoit un suivi régulier des stocks, de leur répartition et de leur renouvellement afin de prévenir les ruptures durant les compétitions. Le dispositif comprend, en outre, un dossier patient informatisé dédié aux JOJ, destiné à renforcer la traçabilité des soins et à faciliter la circulation de l’information médicale. Le ministère de la Santé entend ainsi garantir une prise en charge adaptée des athlètes, des délégations officielles, des spectateurs et des populations, tout en renforçant la prévention et la gestion des urgences sanitaires pendant les Jeux. Salla GUEYE

items.title: Somalie: après plus de 30 ans, l’ONU tourne une page de son engagement politique
items.description: Les Nations Unies mettront fin, le 31 octobre 2026, aux activités de leur Mission d’assistance transitoire en Somalie (UNTMIS). Dans une déclaration publiée, le lundi 26 octobre par son porte-parole, le Secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, a salué les progrès accomplis dans la reconstruction de l’État somalien, tout en appelant à maintenir l’appui international face aux défis sécuritaires et politiques. Une page se tourne dans l’engagement politique des Nations Unies en Somalie. Après plus de trois décennies de missions dans le pays, l’organisation s’apprête à clôturer les activités de l’UNTMIS le 31 octobre 2026, avec un transfert de responsabilités aux institutions somaliennes et aux structures onusiennes présentes sur le terrain. Dans une déclaration rendue publique lundi 26 octobre, António Guterres a salué les avancées enregistrées en matière de paix et de reconstruction de l’État. Il a également mis en avant «la détermination et la résilience du peuple somalien» face aux difficultés persistantes. Créée en novembre 2024 pour succéder à la Mission d’assistance des Nations Unies en Somalie (UNSOM), l’UNTMIS achève cette transition conformément à une feuille de route convenue avec le gouvernement fédéral. Ses fonctions ont été transférées aux institutions nationales ainsi qu’aux agences, fonds et programmes des Nations Unies opérant dans le pays, avec pour objectif de renforcer la prise en main nationale des efforts de consolidation de la paix et de construction de l’État. La fin de la mission ne signifie toutefois pas le retrait de l’ONU. António Guterres a exhorté la communauté internationale à poursuivre son soutien à la Somalie, notamment pour favoriser un dialogue politique inclusif, promouvoir la réconciliation, consolider les institutions et garantir le respect des droits humains. Le défi sécuritaire demeure également majeur. Le Secrétaire général a insisté sur la nécessité de poursuivre la lutte contre Al-Shabaab, groupe islamiste armé qui mène une insurrection contre le gouvernement somalien, et d’accompagner le pays vers une transition sécuritaire progressive et durable. Les Nations Unies entendent ainsi maintenir leur coopération avec les autorités somaliennes, en partenariat avec l’Union africaine et d’autres acteurs internationaux, afin de soutenir la stabilité et le développement du pays. António Guterres a enfin rendu hommage aux représentants spéciaux qui se sont succédé en Somalie, ainsi qu’aux personnels nationaux et internationaux ayant servi au sein de l’UNTMIS et des missions précédentes. Il a salué leur dévouement, souvent dans des conditions extrêmement difficiles, et honoré la mémoire des membres du personnel onusien morts au service de la paix. Le 31 octobre marquera donc la fin d’une mission politique, mais pas celle du partenariat entre l’ONU et la Somalie. La consolidation des acquis, la lutte contre l’insécurité et le renforcement des institutions nationales resteront déterminants pour permettre au pays de construire un avenir pacifique, stable et prospère, conformément à l’engagement réaffirmé par António Guterres. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Somalie: après plus de 30 ans, l’ONU tourne une page de son engagement politique est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Grève du SNESUP, les étudiants s’inquiètent pour leur année universitaire
items.description: Les enseignants de l'enseignement superieur sont en greve depuis le lundi 26 octobre 2026. Le Syndicat national de l'enseignement superieur et de la recherche scientifique (SNESUP) reclame le paiement de la prime de recherche. Prevu pour durer 120 heures, soit cinq jours, le mouvement est renouvelable jusqu'a la satisfaction des revendications syndicales. Une situation qui inquiete les etudiants, preoccupes par les consequences sur leur formation. Amphitheâtres vides, bibliotheques desertes et bureaux fermes. C'est le constat ce mardi matin a la faculte des sciences administratives et politiques (FSAP). Les etudiants redoutent de nouveaux retards dans leur cursus universitaire. etudiant en licence, Souleymane Ongoïba deplore les consequences de ces interruptions repetees sur le parcours universitaire. Quand les greves impactent les projets futurs « Nous sommes la sur la colline depuis 2023 et jusqu'a present, on n'arrive pas a terminer la licence », Souleymane Ongoïba. Il estime que ces retards peuvent egalement compromettre les projets des etudiants, notamment leur participation a certains concours, en raison de l'âge limite requis. L'etudiant souligne aussi les difficultes rencontrees par ceux qui doivent supporter les frais de deplacement pour se rendre a la faculte. Pour lui, la repetition des greves rend la situation particulierement preoccupante. De son cote, Mariam Konate, egalement etudiante en licence, deplore les perturbations dans la preparation des cours et des examens. « S'il y a toujours des greves, on n'arrive meme pas a bien nous preparer. Meme nous sommes en TD (travaux diriges, Ndlr) comme ca, mais certains enseignants ne viennent pas », temoigne-t-elle. Le SNESUP menace de reconduire la greve « Nous sommes ouverts au dialogue. Dans un premier temps, nous avons decrete 120 heures. Si rien n'est fait d'ici la fin de ce delai, nous allons renouveler la greve. Elle sera reconduite autant de fois que le gouvernement restera insensible a nos doleances », declare Dr Oumar Coulibaly, secretaire general du Syndicat national de l'enseignement superieur et de la recherche scientifique. Selon le responsable syndical, aucune negociation n'a encore ete engagee avec les autorites. Le SNESUP previent que la mobilisation se poursuivra dans les etablissements d'enseignement superieur et de recherche tant que ses revendications ne seront pas satisfaites. En attendant une eventuelle issue au conflit, les etudiants restent dans l'incertitude, avec la crainte de voir leur calendrier universitaire davantage perturbe. L’article Grève du SNESUP, les étudiants s’inquiètent pour leur année universitaire est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Egypt: Prominent Journalist Lina Attalah Detained
items.description: Click to expand Image Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of Mada Masr, in Cairo, Egypt, November 24, 2017. © 2017 Roger Anis/AP Photo (Beirut) - The New Cairo Misdemeanor Court convicted Lina Attalah, editor-in-chief of the independent news platform Mada Masr, of operating without a license in a single hearing on October 27, 2026. The court fined her 3 million Egyptian pounds (US$53,474) and ordered the website’s closure. The authorities took Attalah into custody after the hearing. Mada Masr reported that prior to ruling, the judge cleared the courtroom, rejected all procedural motions presented by Attalah’s defense team including requests to present evidence and hear from witnesses, and replaced her defense counsel against her will. Attalah had received a summons on October 19 to appear for questioning before the Supreme State Security Prosecution and Egyptian authorities on October 22 referred her to trial on charges of establishing, managing, and operating a website without a license. The following quote can be attributed to Bassam Khawaja, deputy Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch: “The summary conviction of Lina Attalah in a sham process involving a single, rushed hearing is a complete travesty of justice. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi’s government is clearly determined to wipe out the last remnants of independent media in the country. Egypt’s international partners should loudly condemn this outrageous crackdown.”

items.title: Winners of the European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
items.description: © Audun Rikardsen / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 A Seal’s Worst Nightmare . Highly Commended, Mammals. “For many years, I had been planning to photograph the most common hunting technique of polar bears ( Ursus maritimus ) from a seal’s perspective. In the dense pack ice at 83° N, I drilled a hole next to a seal’s breathing hole, installed my camera beneath it, and positioned a motion sensor on the ice above. Eight hours later, I spotted a polar bear in the distance heading straight for the breathing hole. By then, a thin layer of ice had formed on the water. The bear pushed its head through the ice to see what was going on below and looked straight into the camera. The bear then lay down and slept for nine hours, leaving me unable to retrieve my camera. When the animal finally moved on, I rushed over and was over thrilled to discover that I had captured my dream photo of a polar bear.” © Jan Leßmann and Hermann Hirsch / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Pretty on Pink . Highly Commended, Other Animals. “While staying in the Camargue in the south of France, we came across a group of greater flamingos ( Phoenicopterus roseus ) near Saintes-Maries-de-la-Mer. They were standing in a ditch and weren’t bothered in the least by the people walking past just a few meters away. Anyone who has ever photographed in the Camargue will know this all too well: You set up your camera, compose your image, and within seconds you are swarmed by mosquitoes. This particular mosquito was perched quite attractively on the neck of a resting flamingo.” © Csaba Daroczi / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Water Rocket . Highly Commended, Birds. “This photograph was taken in January at the Kiskunság Lakes in Hungary. As these salt lakes are very shallow, they freeze over every winter and dry out completely in summer. They serve as important breeding and resting habitats for numerous bird species. Because of the mild winter, the ice on the lakes started melting in January. Waterbirds appeared almost immediately—mainly ducks and geese. The drone perspective offered an interesting sight as the birds churned up the mud, creating striking shapes and patterns.” © Danny Green / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Black Wolf. Highly Commended, Mammals. “This image was taken in Yellowstone National Park in the United States, a place I have visited regularly for many years. One of the main reasons for my repeated visits is that there are few better places to observe and photograph wolves ( Canis lupus ). Even so, these animals are elusive and encounters are a matter of luck. Around 50 percent of the wolves in Yellowstone are black, and, although I have seen and photographed them many times before, I always felt that I had not yet captured a truly compelling image. During this particular visit, I encountered the Wapiti Pack which had taken down a bison along Firehole River and consists mostly of black individuals. It was an extraordinary experience, given that wolf sightings in Yellowstone typically last only a few minutes.” © Szymon Bartołd / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Swan Lake . Winner, Youth Category | 14–17 years. “Out walking, I came across a lake with a large number of waterbirds, and decided to return before dawn the next morning. Well hidden, I watched as mute swans ( Cygnus olor ) rose majestically out of the mist in a scene bathed in gold light.” © Henley Spiers / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Turbulent Feeding Patch . Runner-up, Underwater World. “Marine iguanas ( Amblyrhynchus cristatus ) are endemic to the Galápagos Archipelago, Ecuador. They are most often seen basking in the sun, their dark bodies perfectly camouflaged against the black lava rocks. As ectothermic reptiles, they rely on external heat to regulate their body temperature. This is particularly important as they dive into the cold waters surrounding the archipelago to forage, primarily on marine algae. I followed this individual into the water and watched with fascination as it propelled itself swiftly and purposefully through the powerful surf with the aid of its muscular tail. While I was tossed about by the waves, the marine iguana clung firmly to a rock with its sharp claws and began methodically grazing on algae.” © Sandra Kenyon / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Sky Surfer . Highly Commended, Birds. “Each March, tens of thousands of seabirds return to the windswept Arctic island of Hornøya in the Barents Sea for the breeding season. This was my third consecutive visit, as in previous years I had missed this highly synchronized migration event—an experience I was determined to witness at least once. This time, everything came together. The deafening calls and the swirling movements of immense flocks passing just a few meters overhead were truly breathtaking. European shags ( Phalacrocorax aristotelis ) are giants compared to the smaller auks, and as I watched them weaving through the fast-moving streams of common guillemots ( Uria aalge ), I realised there was potential for a striking and dynamic image. When a shag came in to land, perfectly framed by countless guillemots, I was finally able to capture the photograph I had long envisioned.” © Imre Potyó / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Hidden Worlds . Overall Winner. “I have been photographing hibernating bats for 13 years in restricted-access mine tunnels in the Börzsöny mountains of Hungary, and yet this particular composition was novel for me. A key characteristic of the lesser horseshoe bat ( Rhinolophus hipposideros ) is that, during hibernation it occasionally wakes and leaves its roost to hunt flying insects. In doing so, the bat leaves behind droppings that gradually accumulate into a continuous dark layer. And this is where the real wonder begins: in the beam of a torch, a whitish coating can be seen on the guano—a small pin mold thriving in this unusual habitat. Using a macro lens, I captured the mold in the foreground with the hibernating bats visible in the background.” © Preeti John / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Exit Stage Right . Highly Commended, Mammals. “End of a performance in Lake Clark National Park, Alaska: The scene is over, and the grizzly bear ( Ursus arctos horribilis ) has had its moment in the spotlight. The animal leaves the stage without a bow, without a backward glance. Fog hangs like a flowing curtain, and the bokeh glows like fading stage lights. A gull remains behind, watching the main actor’s exit and perhaps wondering what it should do next.” © Jan Wieczorek / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Secret Paths . Winner, Birds. “During moult, common cranes ( Grus grus ) lose all their flight feathers at once, rendering them earthbound for several weeks. During this period, they remain extremely vigilant and usually hide in wet forests where they can find food. At dawn, the cranes walk from their roosting sites via secret paths through reed beds to their feeding grounds and typically return via the same route.” © Bart Heirweg / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Tiny Giants . Highly Commended, Mammals. “This photograph was taken using a drone near the Ilulissat Icefjord on the west coast of Greenland. It shows two humpback whales ( Megaptera novaeangliae ) swimming among drifting ice floes and towering icebergs. The drone was deliberately flown at a higher altitude to place the whales in the context of the wider landscape and to convey the immense scale of their Arctic habitat.” © Agorastos Papatsanis / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Microcosm . Highly Commended, Other Animals. “Sunlight transforms the underside of a fungus ( Pluteus atrotomentosus ) into an architectural masterpiece—a tiny illuminated cathedral. Photographed from an extremely low point of view on the forest floor of Mount Olympus in Greece, the scene takes on an unexpected sense of scale and drama. Beneath the glowing gills, an ant makes its way across the fungus, a subtle reminder of the microfauna that inhabits these miniature worlds.” © Lukas Schaefer / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Helping Hands . Runner-up, Humans and Nature. “During the mating season, capercaillie ( Tetrao urogallus ) sometimes lose their wariness of people, seeing them instead as rivals. That is exactly what happened at a ski resort near my home, where a capercaillie took up position on the ski slope every day throughout the lekking season to defend his patch. The bird soon became something of a local celebrity, even making the news, and crowds came daily to watch and film him. Then, one day, a ski race was held—and the bird chose the middle of the course to display. Not the safest spot. Several people stepped in, gently steering him behind the safety fence and out of harm’s way. A year later, the same bird was accidentally killed by a skier who failed to notice it. Some people care. Others simply don’t.” © Marco Colombo / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Furry Ghost . Highly Commended, Other Animals. “During a nighttime photography expedition along the coast of Sardinia, I discovered this fluorescent hairy crab ( Pilumnus sp. ) in a rock pool, glowing in the beam of my UV torch like a shaggy ghost in the darkness.” © Philipp Egger / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 Rain of Fire . Highly Commended, Nature’s Studio. “During a volcanic eruption, molten lava is thrown out into the dark of night. The glowing arcs trace the paths of liquid rock, hurled skyward by explosive degassing. Shot as a long exposure from a safe distance, these natural movements appear as energy-charged lines. In the lower part of the frame, the ejected fragments cool and begin to solidify within seconds, laying down new crust.” © Lorenzo Shoubridge / European Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 The Cat and a Thousand Lanterns . Winner, Mammals. “In the wild, romantic mountain landscape of Alto Mugello, Italy, a European wildcat ( Felis silvestris ) moves silently through the night, framed by the ethereal dance of countless fireflies. Capturing this fleeting encounter required months of preparation and an almost invisible photographic setup: a DSLR camera trap installed with meticulous care to ensure that the wildlife remained entirely undisturbed.” Be sure to visit the GDT’s website for full coverage of the winners and honorees.

items.title: The Issues Christian Voters Are Neglecting
items.description: E arlier this month the president of the Southern Baptist Convention, Willy Rice , called on pastors to “step up” their political activism as the midterm elections draw near. His argument is that many political issues are, at their heart, moral and theological issues that “strike at the very center of what we believe to be true and what we believe people need to know in order to flourish personally and as a culture.” Rice named four specific issues: abortion, the redefinition of marriage, transgender identity, and illegal immigration. These are the topics that fundamentalists and evangelicals most often invoke as nonnegotiable biblical imperatives, and they are treated as tests of faithfulness. The list is so widely accepted within these subcultures that it is hardly ever questioned. The question worth asking is not why Rice and so many other Christians focus on these issues—some of which, including abortion , I have written about and take seriously—but why they focus on them to the exclusion of others. The answer might tell us something important about what presently stirs fundamentalists and evangelicals to political action and what leaves them unmoved. R ice insists that the issues he prioritizes have to do with human flourishing. He believes that Christians have an obligation to speak out about political and cultural matters that intersect with scriptural truth, morality, and a biblical ethic. And he would insist that the Bible defines his politics, not the other way around. But is that actually true? In addition to the issues on which he chooses to focus, there are others on which Rice and many of those who share his worldview have been silent. Why, for example, have pastors and other Christian leaders who insist that they care about human life and flourishing not spoken out against the dismantling of the U.S. Agency for International Development, carried out by DOGE, and the disruption of the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief? According to modeling estimates by Boston University’s Brooke Nichols, in the first year alone these cuts had resulted in more than three-quarters of a million deaths , more than 500,000 of them children. A study in The Lancet projected that if the USAID cuts are not reversed, they could cause more than 14 million additional deaths by 2030, including some 4.5 million children under age 5. Might not those who claim to be shaped by a Jesus ethic want to speak out and make global development a first-order concern rather than an afterthought? [ Peter Wehner: American Christians face a choice ] Bono, the lead singer of U2 and himself a Christian, cited the Lancet study in a recent interview with The New York Times . “Let’s say they’re half wrong,” he said. “What Christian household, what Catholic household, what Jewish household, anyone of faith, in fact anyone of conscience, would allow the hemorrhaging of human life that is going to happen as a result of these DOGE cuts? It’s unconscionable.” The answer to Bono’s haunting question—Who would allow the hemorrhaging of human life that is going to happen?—is Christians all across America. Why the silence? One could ask the same question about other issues. For example, since 1980, the U.S. Refugee Admissions Program has offered a home to people fleeing war and persecution, many of them Christians. On the first day of his second term, President Trump suspended the program. He then set the refugee ceiling for fiscal year 2026 at a record-low of 7,500, later raising it to 17,500 under an emergency determination but reserving nearly all of those slots for white South Africans, whose claims of persecution are disputed by many independent observers. Meanwhile, Christians facing some of the world’s most severe persecution, in countries such as Afghanistan, Iran, Sudan, and Burma, are largely shut out. The ceiling for fiscal year 2027 remains 17,500, and has the same priority. In 2024, by contrast, the United States resettled more than 100,000 refugees. The president of World Relief, an evangelical humanitarian organization, called the policy “heartbreaking.” He warned that the U.S. has “effectively abandoned” those fleeing horrific religious persecution. Yet very few Christians have said anything about this. Silence has also been the reaction to the assault on medical research. According to Grant Witness , which tracks the federal government’s cancellations and reinstatements of research grants at agencies such as the National Institutes of Health, more than 5,700 NIH grants, with a total value of $15 billion, have been disrupted since April 2025. This includes scores of grants for research on cancer and Alzheimer’s disease, which touch countless families in congregations all across America. Many of those grants were eventually reinstated, but massive harm was done. Some trials can’t be completed, because of the loss of follow-up data; many research groups that come apart can’t be reassembled. Now, ask yourself this: Why don’t these three issues—saving the lives of the world’s poorest children, offering refuge to those fleeing war and persecution, and advancing the research that brings healing to the sick—occupy more attention of politically active Christians? After all, these are not peripheral concerns; they go to the essence of what mattered to Jesus. He told his followers that whatever they did for “the least of these,” they did for him. He counted welcoming the stranger among such acts, and he spent much of his ministry healing the sick and relieving suffering. I don’t claim that these three issues exhaust the concerns Christians should bring to public life, or that mine is the only faithful way to rank them. Thoughtful Christians will weigh things differently. But measured by the lives that could be saved, sheltered, and healed, I do think there is a strong case that they belong near the top of any list shaped by the life and teachings of Jesus. That they so rarely make the list at all shows how deeply the grooves of decades of political activism have been worn. Some issues command instant attention, but others barely register. If Christians were willing to step out of those grooves, even for a moment, they would see how much good could be achieved. Lives could be saved through global health programs, families could find refuge and a new beginning, and cures could come for diseases that inflict suffering on countless people. The question is not whether the Bible speaks to matters of justice and healing. “Nothing about Jesus is more certain historically than that he healed,” the novelist and Presbyterian minister Frederick Buechner wrote . It is whether Christians will let Jesus’s ethic define our politics. S o what explains this selectivity in deciding which political issues have a claim on the Christian conscience? The answer involves a complex mix of factors. One is the vivifying effect of being part of a culture war. Many Christians feel that they are engaged in a righteous struggle against a secular culture that they believe holds them in contempt. Some of their concerns are real and held in good faith: about religious liberty, the protection of unborn life, and the health of families. But the culture wars also offer a black-and-white, us-versus-them moral framework that is especially appealing to people who feel culturally displaced. Saving children in sub-Saharan Africa doesn’t carry the same drama; there is no progressive enemy to defeat. Another factor is an entire media and institutional ecosystem that has every worldly incentive to focus relentlessly on cultural flashpoints, because doing so raises money and drives viewership, clicks, and engagement. Distance plays its own role too. Many people dying from preventable diseases live thousands of miles away. Global health lacks the emotional urgency of social issues that play out close to home. Partisanship also plays a huge part. Political scientists such as Ryan Burge and Michele Margolis argue that, for many white evangelicals, party identity now drives which issues feel religiously urgent. “Politics has become the master identity,” according to Burge . “Everything else lines up behind partisanship.” Even the teachings of Jesus. T he problem runs deeper than issue selection, though. It extends to how scripture itself is interpreted. Many Christians read the Bible through a set of political and cultural assumptions and then present the results as authoritatively “biblical.” The Bible is used to ratify views held for reasons that have little to do with faith. All of us, to varying degrees, are guilty of this. No one has ever read the Bible unfiltered; everyone interprets it. How we do so is shaped by the traditions we embrace—Southern Baptist, Anglicanism, Eastern Orthodoxy, nondenominationalism, Calvinism, Arminianism, fundamentalism, progressivism—and by much else besides. Our family’s origins; the era in which we live; and our nationality, temperament, education, social circles, and psychological makeup shape what we are able to see and not see, and how we process the world. We bring our life experiences and our mental maps to the biblical text, as we do to everything else. The same passage speaks differently to a person in the fourth century or the 14th century than it does to someone in the 21st century, and it speaks differently to every person in the same pew. In Galileo’s day, Christians read Psalm 93:1—“the world also is stablished, that it cannot be moved”—as a literal statement that the Earth does not move, and the verse was invoked against the idea that it orbits the sun. Virtually no Christian reads it that way today. The text did not change; our knowledge of the world did. The same is true of slavery. For most of Christian history, the institution itself went largely unchallenged. Christians criticized particular abuses and particular forms of enslavement, but rarely slavery per se. The most remarkable exception, a fourth-century sermon on Ecclesiastes by Gregory of Nyssa condemning slaveholding outright, had little lasting influence. The first denomination to formally condemn slaveholding was the Quakers, in 1776, more than 1,700 years after Jesus taught his followers to do unto others as they would have others do unto them. The Southern Baptist Convention itself was founded in 1845 in part to defend slaveholding, which its founders insisted that the Bible plainly permitted. The SBC took 150 years to formally repent that history. Every reading of the Bible, and every conception of God, is to some significant degree culturally conditioned. This is a basic reality, and it was true even of the biblical writers, who wrote in the languages, genres, and assumptions of their own times. “If we are to speak of God giving the Scriptures to people,” the eminent Bible scholar John Barton has written, “it can only be in and through the human process.” None of this diminishes Scripture. God’s choice to collaborate with human beings dignifies them in a way that treating them as stenographers would not. The problem, then, comes not from our reading being shaped by our time and place, which is unavoidable, but from failing to acknowledge it. This unwillingness comes from an understandable place. Many Christians fear that conceding the existence of cultural conditioning invites subjectivity into interpretation. But subjectivity is already there; the only question is whether we admit it. Pretending otherwise doesn’t eliminate our biases. It simply hides them, and in doing so makes interpretive mistakes much harder to correct. Part of what makes our own subjectivity so hard to see is a belief, common in many Christian communities, that the Bible is almost entirely self-evident. A friend who attended a respected evangelical seminary once told me that 95 percent or more of scripture is clear—not difficult, not complicated, plain on its face to anyone who reads it. If that is true, then most disagreements are not good-faith differences over interpretation; they are matters of willful blindness or disobedience. If one’s own reading is simply what the Bible says, then anyone who reads it differently is rejecting God’s word. This mindset has done enormous damage, turning honest disagreements into loyalty tests, dividing churches, and telling believers who have difficult questions that they must choose between them and their faith. And at times, it has led to far worse. When people are certain that their reading is simply God’s truth, dissent becomes more than a mistake. It can be seen as a grave error that needs to be punished. As great a figure as Augustine defended the state’s coercion of the Donatists, a schismatic sect, and used verses from the Gospel of Luke to justify it. Thomas Aquinas went further, holding that heretics who persisted after receiving repeated warnings could rightly be handed over to the state “to be exterminated from the world by death.” Centuries later, Voltaire fiercely criticized the intolerance and cruelty that this outlook had produced. In 1766, a 20-year-old French nobleman, the Chevalier de La Barre, was accused of failing to remove his hat as a religious procession passed, singing impious songs, and damaging a wooden crucifix. He was tortured and beheaded, and his body was burned at the stake along with a copy of Voltaire’s Dictionnaire Philosophique nailed to his chest. The claim that the Bible’s teachings on important matters are clear and obvious is belied by the fact that, as the Bible scholar Kenton Sparks and the sociologist Christian Smith have documented, nearly every significant interpretive question yields a variety of readings. Devout Christians have reached different conclusions on baptism, church governance, the Lord’s Supper, and whether the miraculous spiritual gifts have ceased. There are disagreements about the end-times, the nature of the atonement, the role of women in ministry, the balance between works and grace, and whether Genesis offers a literal or figurative account of creation. There are differences over pacifism and just war, how to understand predestination and free will, whether a person can lose their salvation, the age of the Earth, and the nature of heaven and hell. There are thousands of Christian denominations, many of them born of disputes over what scripture teaches. As William Blake put it , “Both read the Bible day and night, / But thou read’st black where I read white.” [ Peter Wehner: The evangelicals who see Trump’s viciousness as a virtue ] The apostle Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, said that “now we see through a glass, darkly.” If that was true of Paul, it is surely true of the rest of us. None of what I’m arguing here means that all readings of the Bible are equally valid, or that some interpretive approaches don’t bring readers closer to the Bible’s truths than others. The German pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer understood what Jesus asked of his followers far better than did Ludwig Müller , the leader of the state-controlled Protestant Reich Church in Nazi Germany. Harriet Beecher Stowe’s views on slavery were much closer to the ethic of the Sermon on the Mount than were those of James Henley Thornwell , the South Carolina Presbyterian theologian who argued that slavery was part of God’s divinely ordained social order. The political theology of former Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams, which sees the Church as a witness within a plural society rather than a power over it, reflects the way of Jesus more faithfully than does that of Doug Wilson, a leading proponent of Christian nationalism who calls for “ mere Christendom .” No one can begin to remotely comprehend the ways and words of a God who created the heavens and the Earth and a reality beyond time. But some come closer than others. O ne of the things that I see more clearly now than I did when I was younger is that discernment matters at least as much as familiarity with Bible verses. It is an immensely important virtue, and an underrated one. Discernment encompasses wisdom, and it protects us from distorting scripture, which is what Satan did in the wilderness when he quoted the Psalms to tempt Jesus, getting the words right and the meaning wrong. Discernment allows us to look beneath the words to grasp their purpose. It is not primarily an intellectual skill, though intellect is involved; it is formed by practice and character, as the writer of Hebrews says of those whose powers of discernment have been “trained by constant practice.” It helps us perceive reality and understand what the moment requires of a faithful person. Discernment also requires humility, a willingness to learn from others rather than merely argue with them, in the conviction that “iron sharpens iron” and that no one sees the whole truth alone. Humility keeps our views open to refinement. But it rarely comes easily, especially for those raised in faith communities that prize certainty. “When you grow up believing that your religious worldview contains the key to absolute truth and provides an answer to every question,” the Christian author Rachel Held Evans wrote , “you never really get over the disappointment of learning that it doesn’t.” The philosopher and theologian David Bentley Hart, in his book Atheist Delusions , writes about the extraordinary revision of the moral and conceptual categories brought about by early Christianity. According to Hart, there emerged from darkness into full visibility “the human person as such, invested with an intrinsic and inviolable dignity, and possessed of infinite value.” A lot has gone wrong in Christian history, and a lot has gone wrong in the here and now. Christianity can be a faith of serrated edges. So many people have been wounded in the name of Jesus. And yet there remains, for those of the Christian faith, the true Jesus—himself a God of wounds, a person of incomprehensible moral beauty who came not to judge the world but to save it. If Christians are going to be active in public life, we would all do well to choose for our master identity Jesus over the gods of this world, who sanctify our political views and the hatreds that fuel them.

items.title: Zone militaire numéro 3 ( Kaolack): Le Colonel Abdoulaye Mbengue installé
items.description: Le chef d’état-major général des Armées, le vice-amiral d’escadre Oumar Wade, a officiellement installé, ce mardi 27 octobre, à Kaolack, le Colonel Abdoulaye Mbengue dans ses fonctions de commandant de la Zone militaire n° 3 de Kaolack. Il succède au Colonel Massamba Thiam. La cérémonie, marquée par une prise d’armes suivie d’un défilé de troupes à pied, s’est déroulée sur le boulevard El Hadj Abdoulaye Niasse, en présence des autorités administratives et religieuses de Kaolack. Instructeur en techniques commandos, diplômé des écoles d’état-major de Chine et du Gabon, le Colonel Mbengue est également diplômé de l’École supérieure de guerre de l’Armée de terre des États-Unis. Avant sa nomination, il dirigeait le Prytanée militaire de Saint-Louis. Le nouveau commandant entend poursuivre et renforcer les acquis en matière de défense du territoire, en mettant l’accent sur la discipline et la préparation opérationnelle des unités. « Il s’agira de les améliorer, en sensibilisant le personnel sur la discipline, mais aussi sur la préparation, afin que, le jour J, les unités soient prêtes à exécuter leur mission », a-t-il déclaré. Face aux menaces sécuritaires, notamment celles observées au Sahel et aux frontières, il a insisté sur l’anticipation et le renseignement pour permettre une réaction rapide avant que les risques n’affectent les populations. Le Colonel Mbengue a enfin appelé les autorités et les populations à renforcer leur coopération avec les forces de défense et de sécurité, soulignant l’importance du partage d’informations pour mieux assurer la protection des personnes et du territoire. Mamadou THIAM (Correspondant)

items.title: La vérité d’une histoire russe
items.description: Testez le Grand Continent . Les idées et les analyses qu’on ne trouve nulle part. Mais que vous verrez bientôt partout. Dans votre boîte mail à partir de 8 euros par mois À mi-chemin de la lecture de ces Mémoires orphelines , nous est revenue à l’esprit la célèbre phrase de Tolstoï qui ouvre Anna Karénine : « Toutes les familles heureuses se ressemblent, mais chaque famille malheureuse l’est à sa façon ». Car toutes les mémoires ne se ressemblent pas, et celles de Nicolas Werth ont une densité, une richesse et une humanité qui les distinguent. Mais Adieu ma Russie est aussi une histoire de famille. Né en 1950, Nicolas Werth est un spécialiste de l’histoire de l’URSS, lui-même fils d’un historien, Alexander Werth, expert de la Russie et de l’URSS qui précède le printemps de Prague. La filiation est essentielle. Elle est même si importante que Nicolas Werth en a fait le fil rouge de ces 389 pages qui s’avouent d’emblée comme une histoire de transmission intellectuelle et d’héritage sensible. « Adieu ma Russie » sont les derniers mots qu’a prononcés Alexander Werth en se donnant la mort après avoir appris l’invasion de la Tchécoslovaquie par les chars soviétiques en 1969. L’événement fut la goutte de sang qui fit déborder le vase de l’espoir. Les Mémoires orphelines du fils commencent par cette disparition, évoquée dans un prologue étonnant de la part d’un historien que la lumière sombre des archives attire plus que celle de l’exposition médiatique : quatorze pages d’un journal d’internement à Sainte-Anne, en juillet 2023, au moment où le fils a flanché. C’était peu après l’invasion de l’Ukraine, la dépression et le désespoir ont failli avoir raison de lui. Commence alors le récit de vie d’un historien qui ne parle pas de lui, mais des autres. Le « je » est presque entièrement absent de son livre, mais la présence du père revient régulièrement. D’abord parce que Nicolas Werth s’est plongé dans une histoire paternelle qu’il ne connaissait guère. Les Werth sont à l’origine des Allemands de la Lettonie russifiée, ce qu’on appelait des barons baltes, installés à Saint-Pétersbourg depuis le début du XIXe siècle. Une famille bourgeoise, aisée et cultivée, qui pencha sans hésitation du côté des Mencheviks lors de la Révolution de 1917. Mais le père d’Alexander Werth n’était pas celui qu’il croyait, c’est donc un secret de famille que le livre dévoile, avec sobriété, sans la mise en scène parfois grandiloquente à laquelle nous a habitués l’autofiction. Un autre secret de famille apparaîtra plus loin, simplement évoqué en note de bas de page. Ensuite parce que le père, naturalisé anglais, fut un historien dont les livres ont été traduits en russe et lus par les Soviétiques, si bien que son nom fut souvent pour le fils un sésame, une façon de mettre en confiance ses interlocuteurs. Dans un pays où régnait et règne encore la défiance, cette reconnaissance fut précieuse. Enfin, parce qu’Alexander Werth appartenait à une autre génération d’historiens de l’URSS, ce qui permet au fils de différencier son approche de la sienne, de mettre en valeur une foi au projet soviétique qu’il ne partage pas. Ce qui les éloigne ? La conscience de la violence qui fut au cœur de ce projet, et dès le début. Nicolas Werth propose des développements infiniment nuancés et étayés sur ses recherches, sur le déchiffrage de sources inédites, l’accès difficile à des archives conservées dans des spetzkhran (fonds spéciaux), la découverte de documents mis sous scellés dans les soutes d’associations officielles, ou officieuses, un matériau qui lui permet peu à peu de prendre la mesure de la cruauté du XXe siècle soviétique. Il cite ses travaux antérieurs pour en expliquer le cheminement et l’intention qui y a présidé, il fait part de fragments de journaux et de notes qu’il a prises en écoutant des témoins plus âgés. Mais il cite également des travaux de son père, publiés et non publiés, et des enquêtes, des recensements, des sondages réalisés par des historiens peu connus dans nos contrées, ainsi que les comptes-rendus des « ethnologues de villages » visant à fixer la tradition orale paysanne avant 1930 et la dékoulakisation, la « dépaysannisation de la paysannerie », une notion empruntée à son ami Viktor Petrovitch Danilov. Il insiste sur « cette spécificité si forte de la production russe post-soviétique : la compilation de recueils de documents d’archives ». Est-ce à cause de la peur de voir les archives se refermer, de l’urgence qu’il y a à conserver et témoigner pour les générations futures ? Oui, dit-il en citant un collègue russe, mais pas uniquement, ajoute-t-il, toujours méfiant vis-à-vis des généralisations. Pour Nicolas Werth, il ne s’agit pas seulement d’école ni de méthodologie – comment fait-on de l’histoire ? Il s’agit d’une certaine vision des hommes et des femmes, des traces qu’ils laissent et de celles qu’on veut laisser pour eux, quand ce n’est pas l’effacement et la mort sans sépulture. L’historien résume cette vision en affirmant que c’est l’histoire sociale qui l’intéresse. Pour le lecteur, qui n’est pas nécessairement un professionnel de l’histoire, cette dimension est particulièrement présente et c’est ce qui fait l’intérêt, voire la force d’âme de cet Adieu ma Russie . Rien n’y est affirmé d’avance ni aussitôt conceptualisé. Nicolas Werth avoue une certaine réticence vis-à-vis des grandes théories, y compris celles des penseurs du totalitarisme les plus connus. L’on trouvera donc peu de théories dans son livre, mais une longue réflexion nourrie de rencontres avec des êtres de chair et d’os qui font ce qu’ils peuvent pour vivre et survivre, souvent avec un entrain inattendu et impressionnant. Nicolas Werth, l’homme, pas seulement l’historien, évoque avec prodigalité les amis sans lesquels il n’aurait rien pu faire, ni obtenir, ni comprendre. Bien sûr, la répression et la brutalité du contexte confèrent à ces amitiés une valeur qu’elles n’ont peut-être pas dans nos pays, même s’il faut se méfier de l’héroïsation. Tout de même, ses Mémoires orphelines sont ponctuées de brèves biographies d’hommes et de femmes dont les vies tiennent souvent du miracle, qui font de ces mémoires un livre incarné, vivant, doué d’une grande puissance d’émotion. Il y a les collègues, mais aussi les amis peintres, musiciens, écrivains, scientifiques, linguistes… qui puisent en eux une vitalité inouïe. Le livre est un témoignage de première main sur la façon dont l’association Memorial s’est montée. Mentionnons Arsenii Roginski, figure particulièrement attachante : né dans le camp de Velsk, près d’Archangelsk, en 1946, son père, ingénieur, juif, fut arrêté une première fois pendant la Grande Terreur, puis une autre, et encore une autre, tandis que son fils, grandissant dans une petite ville concentrationnaire, « en allant à l’école, ne cessait de croiser des files compactes de détenus encadrés par des gardes se rendant au travail forcé. » Gamin des rues, il semble avoir été sauvé par le théâtre, la, poésie, les amis écrivains et son intelligence humaine et intellectuelle. Arrêté en 1981, il passa quatre ans en prison où il se fit observateur et parlait « avec son humour si fin, écrit Werth, de sa “grande expédition ethnographique”. » Pour Nicolas Werth, ces portraits sont l’occasion de distiller une analyse extrêmement précise des diverses façons de se protéger de la broyeuse d’un pouvoir qui entend contrôler jusqu’à la vie intérieure. Sans systématisme, minutieusement, il met en avant un éventail très serré de poches de liberté que certains arrivent à créer : ici, la micro-résistance du monde paysan dans les années 1930 ; là, les cuisines et les revues comme « espaces de micro-autonomie » ; les réseaux invisibles qui finissent par ouvrir une brèche, aujourd’hui encore… L’historien introduit la notion de « quant-à-soi » pour qualifier l’intériorisation d’une distance par rapport à un système dans lequel on est intégré, qu’il distingue de la dissidence active. Il tente d’appréhender, dit-il, « cette forme singulière de non-adhésion aux valeurs du régime » en empruntant à l’historiographie du nazisme la notion de resistenz . Ce faisant, lui-même introduit une large palette de mots russes en version naturaliter (originale), dont beaucoup sont des intraduisibles tant ils sont attachés à des spécificités et des particularismes de la culture soviétique : les kapstrany et les sotsstrany (les pays capitalistes et les pays socialistes) ; la propiska , le droit de résidence dans une ville, obtenu auprès de la police ; dans un registre plus léger, les gastronomy (les magasins d’alimentation). Les termes évoluent suivant l’époque, y compris la nôtre, certains apparaissent, d’autres disparaissent et sont désormais signes du passé, mais il reste la falsification, les notions conçues pour tordre le cou à la vérité et verser du mensonge. Étonnamment, l’historien finit en avouant ne pas avoir cru ses amis pressentant l’invasion russe du 24 février 2022. Trop d’espoir ? Trop d’amour pour la Russie ? Déni d’un Européen « gâté à la paix » ? Deux mois avant, l’association Memorial avait été dissoute : « prélude à la guerre », évidemment, écrit Nicolas Werth aujourd’hui. Pour un regard extérieur, en revanche, ses confessions font valoir un « sens » qui permet de prendre la mesure de ce qui se joue sous nos yeux, même si ce serait trahir Nicolas Werth que de conclure ainsi. Car son livre recèle ce que les géologues appellent des diamants « super-profonds », des gemmes qui se forment à quelques centaines de kilomètres sous la surface du sol. Ils brillent d’un éclat qui autorise à imaginer moins de mensonge et plus de liberté. L’article La vérité d’une histoire russe est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Le Maroc progresse dans le classement africain de l’attractivité des investissements
items.description: Le Maroc a réalisé une progression remarquable en se hissant au quatrième rang des destinations d’investissement les plus attractives du continent africain, porté par des années d’industrialisation et une croissance économique plus rapide, a indiqué la banque Rand Merchant Bank (RMB), filiale du groupe financier sud-africain FirstRand. Le Maroc est le seul pays à progresser...
